readings.title: The Silent Loss of Languages
readings.summaryVi: Nhiều ngôn ngữ đang biến mất do áp lực kinh tế và xã hội; mất ngôn ngữ là mất tri thức văn hóa, và nỗ lực phục hồi cần cộng đồng chủ động tham gia.
readings.summaryEn: Many languages are disappearing under economic and social pressure; losing a language means losing cultural knowledge, and revival efforts need communities to take an active part.
readings.text:
Linguists broadly agree that a substantial proportion of the world's languages are at risk of disappearing within the coming generations. Unlike the extinction of a plant or animal species, however, the loss of a language rarely attracts headlines. It tends to occur quietly, as each successive generation uses the ancestral tongue a little less until, eventually, no fluent speakers remain.

The forces driving this decline are rarely a matter of deliberate prohibition alone, although historical policies of forced assimilation have certainly played a part in many regions. More commonly, the shift is propelled by economic and social pressures. Parents who perceive a dominant language as the key to education and employment may choose not to pass on their own, believing they are acting in their children's best interests. Urban migration, mass media and the internet can accelerate this process by exposing young people predominantly to a handful of global languages.

Why should such losses matter? One argument is that each language encodes a distinctive way of categorising experience. Vocabulary relating to local plants, weather patterns or kinship structures may embody knowledge accumulated over centuries, some of which is not documented anywhere else. When a language vanishes, this intangible heritage may disappear with it. Moreover, for many communities, language is inseparable from identity, and its erosion can be experienced as a profound cultural dislocation.

Efforts at revitalisation have produced mixed outcomes. Documentation projects, in which researchers record speakers and compile dictionaries, preserve valuable material but do not in themselves create new speakers. More ambitious initiatives, such as immersion schools where children are taught entirely in the endangered language, have reportedly achieved notable success in certain contexts. Nevertheless, such programmes demand sustained funding and, crucially, the commitment of the community itself.

The prevailing view among specialists is that external intervention can support, but never substitute for, local motivation. A language survives not because it is archived, but because people continue to choose to speak it in their daily lives.

questions.q: Language loss usually receives as much media attention as species extinction.
questions.explain: Bài viết: the loss of a language "rarely attracts headlines", trái với ý của câu → FALSE.

questions.q: Some parents stop passing on their language because they think it will help their children.
questions.explain: Bài viết: parents may choose not to pass on their own, "believing they are acting in their children's best interests" → TRUE.

questions.q: Immersion schools are cheaper to run than documentation projects.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói trường immersion "demand sustained funding", không so sánh chi phí với dự án ghi chép → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of documentation projects, according to the passage?
options: They fail to preserve traditional vocabulary and cultural knowledge.
They do not in themselves create new speakers.
They face strong resistance from the younger generation in cities.
They require communities to give up their ancestral identity.
questions.explain: Tác giả chỉ ra rằng các dự án tư liệu hóa lưu giữ tư liệu quý nhưng bản thân chúng không tự tạo ra người nói mới; các phương án khác mâu thuẫn với nội dung bài.

questions.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: Language loss can be effectively halted through comprehensive archiving.
Revitalisation efforts will surely fail without substantial state funding.
A language survives only if people keep choosing to use it.
Immersion schooling is the single practical solution for endangered tongues.
questions.explain: Tác giả kết luận ở câu cuối rằng một ngôn ngữ tồn tại không phải nhờ việc lưu trữ tài liệu mà vì người dân tiếp tục chủ động sử dụng nó trong đời sống ("because people continue to choose to speak it").

readings.title: The Growing Problem of Space Debris
readings.summaryVi: Rác vũ trụ quanh Trái Đất ngày càng nhiều, đe dọa vệ tinh và đòi hỏi cả giải pháp kỹ thuật lẫn hợp tác quốc tế.
readings.summaryEn: Space debris around the Earth keeps increasing, threatening satellites and calling for both technical solutions and international cooperation.
readings.text:
Since the first artificial satellite was launched in the late 1950s, the region of space surrounding the Earth has become increasingly congested. Alongside functioning spacecraft, it now contains a vast quantity of debris: defunct satellites, discarded rocket stages, and countless fragments produced by collisions and explosions. Because these objects travel at extremely high velocities, even a fragment no larger than a fingernail can inflict serious damage on an operational satellite.

Of particular concern is a scenario sometimes referred to as cascading collisions. The theory proposes that, once the density of debris in a given orbit exceeds a critical threshold, each collision would generate further fragments, which would in turn trigger additional collisions. In its most extreme form, this chain reaction could render certain orbits unusable for decades, jeopardising services on which modern societies have come to depend, including weather forecasting, navigation and global communications.

The rapid expansion of commercial activity has intensified these anxieties. Several companies are deploying large constellations of small satellites to provide internet access, and while operators generally design these craft to descend and burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their lifespan, the sheer number of launches inevitably raises the probability of accidents.

Engineers have proposed an array of mitigation strategies. Some focus on prevention, such as ensuring that satellites carry sufficient fuel to move themselves out of busy orbits once their missions conclude. Others concentrate on active removal, with concepts ranging from robotic arms and nets to harpoons capable of capturing derelict objects. Most of these techniques, however, remain at an experimental stage, and their cost is considerable relative to the size of the problem.

Perhaps the most formidable obstacle is not technical but political. Space is a shared environment, yet no single authority has the power to enforce rules across all nations and companies. Existing guidelines are largely voluntary, and compliance varies. Many analysts therefore contend that meaningful progress will depend on stronger international cooperation and a shared recognition that orbital space is a finite resource.

questions.q: Even very small fragments of debris can damage working satellites.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "even a fragment no larger than a fingernail can inflict serious damage on an operational satellite" → TRUE.

questions.q: Commercial satellite operators usually design their craft to remain in orbit permanently.
questions.explain: Bài viết: operators design craft "to descend and burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their lifespan" → FALSE.

questions.q: Harpoons have already been used successfully to remove large amounts of debris.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói các kỹ thuật như harpoon "remain at an experimental stage", không đề cập đã thành công trên quy mô lớn → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What does the theory of cascading collisions suggest?
options: Collisions could produce more fragments and further collisions.
Debris will soon fall back to Earth naturally.
Satellites will become cheaper to launch.
Only old satellites are at risk.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "each collision would generate further fragments, which would in turn trigger additional collisions" → đáp án đúng: Collisions could produce more fragments and further collisions..

questions.q: According to the writer, what is the greatest obstacle to solving the problem?
options: A shortage of qualified engineers to design removal systems.
The extreme velocity of space debris fragments.
General public’s indifference toward space environmental concerns.
Political issues and the absence of a single authority
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the most formidable obstacle is not technical but political... no single authority has the power to enforce rules" → đáp án đúng: Political issues and the absence of a single authority.

readings.title: Ageing Populations and Healthcare
readings.summaryVi: Dân số già hóa gây áp lực lên hệ thống y tế; các giải pháp gồm phòng bệnh, chăm sóc tại cộng đồng và công nghệ, nhưng đều có hạn chế.
readings.summaryEn: An ageing population puts pressure on health systems; solutions include prevention, community care and technology, but each has its limits.
readings.text:
Across much of the world, populations are growing older. Rising life expectancy, combined with declining birth rates, means that the proportion of people over the age of sixty-five is increasing steadily in many countries. While this demographic shift is in many respects a testament to advances in medicine and living standards, it also poses profound challenges for healthcare systems that were largely designed around the treatment of acute, short-term illness.

Older adults are more likely to live with chronic conditions, such as heart disease, diabetes and arthritis, and many experience several of these simultaneously. Managing multiple long-term conditions tends to be both complex and costly, requiring ongoing monitoring, numerous medications and coordination between different specialists. Consequently, health economists frequently warn that expenditure may rise faster than the revenue available to fund it, particularly where a shrinking working-age population contributes a smaller share of taxes.

In response, many policymakers advocate a reorientation towards prevention. Encouraging physical activity, balanced nutrition and social engagement throughout life may postpone the onset of disability and reduce dependence on hospital services. Equally, there is growing interest in delivering care within the community rather than in hospitals. Home visits, local clinics and support for family carers are often regarded as more humane and potentially less expensive, although their effectiveness depends heavily on adequate staffing and funding.

Technology is frequently presented as part of the solution. Remote monitoring devices, for instance, can alert medical teams to changes in a patient's condition, while telemedicine allows consultations without the need to travel. Nevertheless, such innovations are not a panacea. Some older people lack the confidence or resources to use digital tools, and there is a risk that technology could exacerbate isolation if it replaces, rather than complements, human contact.

Ultimately, adapting to an ageing society will require more than incremental adjustments. It calls for a fundamental rethinking of how care is organised, financed and delivered, so that longer lives can also be healthier and more fulfilling ones.

questions.q: Many current healthcare systems were mainly designed to treat short-term illness.
questions.explain: Bài viết: systems "were largely designed around the treatment of acute, short-term illness" → TRUE.

questions.q: Community-based care is always cheaper than hospital treatment.
questions.explain: Bài viết chỉ nói "potentially less expensive" và hiệu quả phụ thuộc vào nhân lực, kinh phí, nên không phải "always" → FALSE.

questions.q: Most older people prefer telemedicine to face-to-face appointments.
questions.explain: Bài không đề cập sở thích của người cao tuổi giữa khám từ xa và khám trực tiếp → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might healthcare spending become difficult to fund?
options: A smaller working-age population contributes a smaller share of taxes.
Chronic illnesses among older patients can no longer be managed.
Advanced digital tools completely replace needed medical personnel.
Community clinics cost significantly more than traditional hospitals.
questions.explain: Đoạn 2 nêu rõ chi phí y tế có nguy cơ vượt quá nguồn thu ngân sách do lực lượng lao động trong độ tuổi suy giảm đóng góp ít thuế hơn.

questions.q: What risk of technology does the writer mention?
options: It makes long-term monitoring far more expensive than hospital care.
It requires vulnerable patients to travel regularly for consultations.
It prevents medical personnel from detecting sudden bodily changes.
It may increase isolation if it replaces human contact.
questions.explain: Đoạn 4 chỉ ra rủi ro công nghệ có thể làm tăng sự cô lập nếu nó thay thế thay vì bổ trợ cho tiếp xúc giữa con người ("could exacerbate isolation if it replaces, rather than complements, human contact").

readings.title: Artificial Intelligence at the Bedside
readings.summaryVi: Trí tuệ nhân tạo đọc ảnh y khoa ngang chuyên gia, nhưng phụ thuộc dữ liệu huấn luyện, thiếu minh bạch và chưa rõ trách nhiệm; giới chuyên môn xem AI là trợ lý chứ không thay thế bác sĩ.
readings.summaryEn: Artificial intelligence can read medical images as well as specialists, but it depends on its training data, lacks transparency and leaves responsibility unclear; experts see AI as an assistant, not a replacement for doctors.
readings.text:
Few fields illustrate both the promise and the pitfalls of artificial intelligence as vividly as medicine. Algorithms trained on vast collections of medical images can now identify certain cancers, eye diseases and fractures with an accuracy that rivals, and occasionally surpasses, that of experienced specialists. Enthusiasts envisage a future in which AI relieves overstretched doctors of routine tasks, catches diseases earlier and extends high-quality diagnosis to regions where specialists are scarce.

The appeal is easy to understand. A radiologist may examine hundreds of scans in a single shift, and fatigue inevitably increases the risk of error. An algorithm does not tire, and it can be deployed to flag suspicious images for priority review, allowing human experts to concentrate their attention where it is most needed. Beyond imaging, machine-learning systems are being used to predict which hospital patients are at risk of sudden deterioration, to speed up the discovery of new drugs and to transcribe consultations so that clinicians spend less time on paperwork.

Nevertheless, translating impressive laboratory results into real clinical benefit has proved more difficult than early headlines suggested. An algorithm is only as reliable as the data on which it was trained. If those data come predominantly from one population, the system may perform poorly for patients of different ethnic backgrounds, ages or sexes, thereby reinforcing existing inequalities in care. Systems that perform well in the hospital where they were developed have, in several documented cases, deteriorated markedly when introduced elsewhere, owing to differences in equipment or patient populations.

Transparency poses a further challenge. Many advanced models operate as so-called "black boxes", producing a conclusion without a readily interpretable explanation. Clinicians may be reluctant to act on a recommendation they cannot scrutinise, and patients are entitled to understand how decisions about their care are reached. There is also the unresolved question of accountability: if an AI-assisted diagnosis proves wrong, it is not obvious whether responsibility lies with the doctor, the hospital or the developer.

For these reasons, most experts envisage AI as an assistant rather than a replacement. Studies suggest that the combination of human judgement and algorithmic support frequently outperforms either alone, provided that clinicians remain alert to the risk of automation bias, the tendency to accept a machine's output uncritically. Regulators, meanwhile, are developing frameworks that require rigorous testing across diverse populations and continuous monitoring after deployment.

The ultimate test of medical AI will not be its performance in controlled trials, but whether it measurably improves outcomes for patients while preserving the trust on which the relationship between doctor and patient depends.

questions.q: Some algorithms can identify certain diseases as accurately as experienced specialists.
questions.explain: Bài viết: algorithms identify some diseases "with an accuracy that rivals, and occasionally surpasses, that of experienced specialists" → TRUE.

questions.q: An AI system that works well in one hospital will perform equally well in every other hospital.
questions.explain: Bài viết: some systems "deteriorated markedly when introduced elsewhere" → FALSE.

questions.q: Most hospitals have already replaced radiologists with algorithms.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu quan điểm của giới chuyên môn rằng AI là trợ lý, không cho biết các bệnh viện đã thay thế bác sĩ hay chưa → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is "automation bias"?
options: The failure of algorithms to explain their diagnostic decisions
The reliance on training data drawn from a single population
The tendency to accept a machine's output uncritically
The diagnostic errors caused by physician fatigue during shifts
questions.explain: Đoạn 5 định nghĩa trực tiếp 'automation bias' là "the tendency to accept a machine's output uncritically" (khuynh hướng tin theo kết quả của máy móc mà thiếu sự phản biện).

questions.q: Why might an algorithm reinforce inequalities in care?
options: It requires costly equipment that many low‑budget hospitals cannot afford.
Its training data may come mainly from one population.
Physicians often distrust the system and decline to adopt it.
The algorithm is unable to interpret complex radiological scans accurately.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "If those data come predominantly from one population, the system may perform poorly for patients of different ethnic backgrounds, ages or sexes" → đáp án đúng: Its training data may come mainly from one population..

readings.title: Beyond Silk: The Ancient Trade Routes of Asia
readings.summaryVi: Con đường tơ lụa thực chất là mạng lưới tuyến đường bộ và biển kéo dài hàng thế kỷ, truyền bá không chỉ hàng hóa mà cả tôn giáo, kỹ thuật làm giấy – và cả dịch bệnh.
readings.summaryEn: The Silk Road was really a network of land and sea routes lasting for centuries, spreading not only goods but also religions, papermaking – and even disease.
readings.text:
The term "Silk Road" conjures up images of camel caravans crossing deserts laden with precious fabric. The reality was considerably more complex. Rather than a single road, it was a shifting network of overland and maritime routes that, over roughly fifteen centuries, linked China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East and the Mediterranean. Silk was merely one commodity among many; spices, horses, paper, glass, precious metals and ceramics all changed hands along the way.

Strikingly, few merchants ever travelled the entire distance. Goods typically passed through a relay of traders, each covering a particular segment before selling to the next. Oasis cities such as Samarkand flourished as hubs where merchants rested, exchanged goods and gathered intelligence about prices and political conditions further along the route. This fragmented structure meant that prices multiplied with every transaction, which is partly why silk commanded such extraordinary value in Rome.

The significance of these routes, however, extended far beyond commerce. Ideas, technologies and beliefs travelled alongside merchandise. Buddhism spread from India into China via Central Asian trading communities, while papermaking techniques gradually moved westward, eventually transforming record-keeping and scholarship in the Islamic world and later in Europe. Musical instruments, artistic motifs and agricultural crops were similarly diffused, leaving traces that historians still detect in surviving artefacts.

Not every exchange was beneficial. Many historians believe that the trade networks facilitated the transmission of disease, most notoriously the plague that devastated Europe and parts of Asia in the fourteenth century. The very connectivity that enabled prosperity also rendered distant populations vulnerable to shared catastrophes.

The decline of the overland routes is often attributed to the expansion of European sea voyages from the late fifteenth century, which allowed goods to be transported in bulk more cheaply by ship. Yet scholars increasingly emphasise that maritime trade across the Indian Ocean had long been substantial, and that political fragmentation and conflict in Central Asia also played a role. The story, once again, resists simple explanations.

Today the Silk Road enjoys renewed prominence, not least because modern infrastructure projects deliberately invoke its legacy. Historians caution, however, against romanticising the past. The ancient routes were neither centrally planned nor consistently peaceful; their enduring importance lies instead in demonstrating how sustained contact between distant societies can reshape economies, cultures and even the course of history itself.

questions.q: Most merchants travelled the whole distance between China and the Mediterranean.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "few merchants ever travelled the entire distance" – hàng hóa được chuyển qua nhiều chặng thương nhân → FALSE.

questions.q: Papermaking techniques moved gradually westward along the trade routes.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "papermaking techniques gradually moved westward" → TRUE.

questions.q: Samarkand was the largest city on the Silk Road.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu Samarkand là một trung tâm phát triển mạnh, không so sánh quy mô với các thành phố khác → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why did silk become so valuable in Rome?
options: Roman authorities strictly limited the entry of foreign textiles.
Dangerous sea routes frequently resulted in lost merchant fleets.
The Chinese empire produced only tiny amounts of fine fabrics.
Prices multiplied with every transaction along the relay of traders.
questions.explain: Đoạn văn chỉ rõ cấu trúc trung chuyển phân mảnh khiến "prices multiplied with every transaction", giải thích vì sao lụa có giá rất cao ở Rome; các lý do về hạn chế nhập khẩu hay vận chuyển đường biển đều không được nêu.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the decline of the overland routes?
options: It had several causes, including conflict in Central Asia.
It was entirely due to the rise of European naval routes.
It resulted primarily from outbreaks of fourteenth-century plague.
It happened abruptly following the collapse of Chinese dynasties.
questions.explain: Đoạn 5 nêu rõ sự suy giảm không chỉ do các chuyến hải hành của châu Âu mà còn vì phân mảnh chính trị và xung đột ở Trung Á ("political fragmentation and conflict in Central Asia also played a role"), bác bỏ quan điểm cho rằng nó chỉ bắt nguồn từ đường biển.

readings.title: The Attention Economy
readings.summaryVi: Khi sự chú ý trở thành tài nguyên khan hiếm, các nền tảng số được thiết kế để giữ chân người dùng – gây phân mảnh sự tập trung và lan truyền tin sai; giải pháp bền vững có thể nằm ở mô hình kinh doanh.
readings.summaryEn: When attention becomes a scarce resource, digital platforms are designed to keep users hooked – fragmenting concentration and spreading misinformation; a lasting solution may lie in the business model.
readings.text:
In an age of information abundance, the scarce resource is no longer information itself but the human attention required to consume it. This insight, articulated by economists decades before the smartphone, underpins what is now termed the attention economy. Many of the most valuable companies in the world offer their core services free of charge; their revenue derives instead from capturing users' time and selling access to it, chiefly through advertising.

The commercial logic has profound consequences for design. If profit depends on engagement, platforms have a powerful incentive to maximise the time users spend on them. Features such as infinite scrolling, autoplaying videos and notifications delivered at unpredictable intervals have been criticised for exploiting well-documented psychological tendencies. Variable rewards, such as the uncertain prospect of a new message or a burst of approval, are known to be particularly compelling, a principle long familiar to designers of gambling machines.

Critics contend that the cumulative effect is a fragmentation of attention. Constant switching between tasks appears to impose a cognitive cost, reducing the capacity for the sustained, deep concentration on which complex reasoning and creative work depend. Some researchers have linked heavy social media use to anxiety and poor sleep, particularly among adolescents, although establishing causation remains notoriously difficult: it is plausible that people who are already anxious gravitate towards their screens.

Moreover, the content that captures attention most effectively is not necessarily the most accurate or valuable. Algorithms that prioritise engagement may inadvertently amplify sensational, divisive or misleading material, since such content provokes strong reactions. This dynamic has prompted concern about the health of public debate and the spread of misinformation.

Responses have emerged on several fronts. Some technology companies have introduced tools that allow users to monitor their screen time or disable certain features. Legislators in various jurisdictions are scrutinising design practices that may be manipulative, especially where children are concerned. At the individual level, a growing movement advocates "digital minimalism", which means deliberately limiting the role of technology to activities that genuinely serve one's values.

Yet framing the issue purely as a matter of individual willpower may be misguided. When some of the most sophisticated engineering in history is devoted to capturing attention, expecting each user to resist unaided seems unrealistic. A more durable solution may require rethinking the underlying business models, so that the commercial success of digital services is aligned with, rather than opposed to, the wellbeing of the people who use them.

questions.q: Many companies in the attention economy earn money mainly from advertising.
questions.explain: Bài viết: their revenue comes from "capturing users' time and selling access to it, chiefly through advertising" → TRUE.

questions.q: Researchers have proved that social media directly causes anxiety in adolescents.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "establishing causation remains notoriously difficult" – chưa chứng minh được quan hệ nhân quả → FALSE.

questions.q: Digital minimalism is more popular among older adults than among young people.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói phong trào này đang phát triển, không so sánh theo độ tuổi → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why are variable rewards described as compelling?
options: Their regular delivery provides a soothing routine, helping people relax.
Their uncertainty makes them particularly attractive, as in gambling machines.
Their educational value encourages deeper reflection, enhancing personal growth.
Their financial value guarantees substantial returns, benefiting users directly.
questions.explain: Bài đọc nêu rõ variable rewards là 'particularly compelling' vì người dùng đối mặt với 'uncertain prospect', tương tự cách thức hoạt động của máy đánh bạc; các phương án còn lại miêu tả sai bản chất ngẫu nhiên này.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest in the final paragraph?
options: Individuals must rely on stronger self‑discipline to limit usage.
Regulators ought to prohibit smartphone ownership for people over eighteen.
Business models may need to be rethought to align with users' wellbeing.
Companies should eliminate all advertising revenue from their platforms.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "A more durable solution may require rethinking the underlying business models" → đáp án đúng: Business models may need to be rethought to align with users' wellbeing..

readings.title: Rewilding: Letting Nature Take the Lead
readings.summaryVi: Tái hoang dã khôi phục các quá trình tự nhiên bằng cách đưa loài như hải ly, sói trở lại; cách tiếp cận này đầy tham vọng nhưng gây tranh cãi và cần sự đồng thuận của cộng đồng.
readings.summaryEn: Rewilding restores natural processes by bringing back species such as beavers and wolves; the approach is ambitious but controversial and needs the agreement of local communities.
readings.text:
For much of the twentieth century, nature conservation in many countries focused on protecting particular species or preserving landscapes in a carefully managed state. Rewilding represents a markedly different philosophy. Rather than intervening continually to maintain a fixed condition, it seeks to restore natural processes and then, as far as possible, allow ecosystems to regulate themselves.

Central to rewilding is the reintroduction of species that once shaped their environments but disappeared because of hunting or habitat loss. Large predators and so-called ecosystem engineers often attract the most attention. The beaver, for instance, builds dams that slow the flow of rivers, creating wetlands that store water, reduce downstream flooding and support a remarkable diversity of insects, birds and amphibians. Similarly, the return of grazing animals such as wild cattle or horses can create a patchwork of open ground and woodland that benefits a wide range of plants.

The most frequently cited example is the reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the 1990s. According to a widely publicised account, wolves reduced the number of elk and altered their behaviour, allowing riverside vegetation to recover, which in turn stabilised riverbanks. Subsequent research, however, has suggested that this "trophic cascade" was considerably more complex and less dramatic than popular versions implied, with factors such as human hunting and drought also playing significant roles. The episode serves as a reminder that ecological outcomes are rarely as tidy as compelling narratives suggest.

Rewilding is not without its detractors. Farmers sometimes fear that returning predators will attack livestock, and beavers can flood valuable agricultural land. Critics also question whether a "wild" state can meaningfully be defined in landscapes that have been shaped by humans for thousands of years. Which point in history, they ask, should serve as the baseline? Proponents generally respond that the aim is not to recreate a specific past, but to increase the complexity and resilience of ecosystems.

Practical success therefore depends as much on social acceptance as on ecology. Projects that compensate farmers for losses, involve local communities in planning and create opportunities in nature tourism tend to encounter less opposition. In densely populated regions, rewilding may take more modest forms, such as allowing rivers to follow their natural courses or leaving parts of farmland to regenerate naturally.

As biodiversity continues to decline globally, rewilding offers an ambitious, if contested, vision: one in which human beings act less as managers of nature and more as facilitators of its recovery.

questions.q: Rewilding aims to keep landscapes in a fixed, carefully managed state.
questions.explain: Bài viết: rewilding seeks to restore natural processes "rather than intervening continually to maintain a fixed condition" → FALSE.

questions.q: Later research suggested that the effects of wolves in Yellowstone were more complex than popular accounts claimed.
questions.explain: Bài viết: nghiên cứu sau này cho thấy "trophic cascade" ở Yellowstone "was considerably more complex and less dramatic than popular versions implied" → TRUE.

questions.q: Beavers have been reintroduced to every country in Europe.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ giải thích vai trò của hải ly, không nói chúng được đưa trở lại những quốc gia nào → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why is the beaver described as an ecosystem engineer?
options: Its feeding habits control invasive vegetation throughout rivers.
Its predation directly limits the numbers of browsing herbivores.
Its dams create wetlands that support many species.
Its burrows aerate surrounding soil and prevent massive erosion.
questions.explain: Tác giả gọi hải ly là kỹ sư hệ sinh thái vì hoạt động đắp đập của chúng tạo ra các vùng đất ngập nước giúp duy trì đa dạng sinh học phong phú.

questions.q: According to the text, which factor helps rewilding projects meet less opposition?
options: Compensating farmers for losses
Keeping local people out of planning
Introducing as many predators as possible
Avoiding nature tourism
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Projects that compensate farmers for losses, involve local communities in planning and create opportunities in nature tourism tend to encounter less opposition" → đáp án đúng: Compensating farmers for losses.

readings.title: The Curious Power of the Placebo
readings.summaryVi: Hiệu ứng giả dược cho thấy kỳ vọng và bối cảnh điều trị có thể tạo ra thay đổi sinh lý thật; mặt trái của nó là hiệu ứng nocebo, và giả dược không thể thay thế thuốc thật.
readings.summaryEn: The placebo effect shows that expectations and the treatment setting can cause real physical changes; its downside is the nocebo effect, and placebos cannot replace real medicine.
readings.text:
In clinical research, the placebo, an inert substance such as a sugar pill, has traditionally been regarded as little more than a methodological tool. By comparing a new drug with a placebo, researchers can determine whether any improvement is attributable to the medication itself. Yet the placebo effect, the genuine improvement that some patients experience after receiving an inactive treatment, has increasingly become an object of study in its own right.

The phenomenon is most pronounced for symptoms that are subjective and influenced by the brain, such as pain, nausea and fatigue. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when patients expect pain relief, regions associated with the body's own pain-control system become more active, and the release of natural painkilling chemicals can increase. In other words, expectation is not merely imaginary; it can produce measurable physiological changes.

Context appears to matter enormously. Experiments have found that injections tend to produce stronger placebo responses than pills, that two pills can outperform one, and that branded or more expensive-looking tablets may be more effective than plain ones. The manner of the practitioner also plays a part: patients treated by a warm, attentive clinician frequently report greater improvement than those receiving identical treatment in a brisk, impersonal manner.

Perhaps the most counterintuitive findings concern so-called open-label placebos. In several trials, patients with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome were explicitly told that they were receiving inactive pills, yet many still reported significant relief. Researchers speculate that the ritual of taking medication, combined with a credible explanation of how placebos can work, may be sufficient to trigger beneficial responses, although these studies have generally been small.

The placebo effect has a less welcome counterpart: the nocebo effect, in which negative expectations produce real side effects. Participants warned about possible symptoms are more likely to experience them, even when they have been given an inactive substance. This poses a genuine dilemma for doctors, who are obliged to inform patients of risks while avoiding the unintended creation of symptoms.

It is important not to overstate the power of placebos. They do not shrink tumours or cure infections, and relying on them in place of effective treatment would be dangerous. Their relevance lies elsewhere. A clearer understanding of how expectation and context influence recovery could help clinicians communicate more effectively and design care that maximises the benefits of genuinely active treatments.

questions.q: Placebo effects are strongest for subjective symptoms such as pain and nausea.
questions.explain: Bài viết: the phenomenon "is most pronounced for symptoms that are subjective and influenced by the brain, such as pain, nausea and fatigue" → TRUE.

questions.q: Placebos can cure infections if patients believe in them.
questions.explain: Bài viết: placebos "do not shrink tumours or cure infections" → FALSE.

questions.q: Open-label placebos are now widely prescribed by family doctors.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói về một số thử nghiệm nhỏ, không đề cập việc bác sĩ gia đình kê đơn giả dược → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the nocebo effect?
options: Improvement observed after receiving an inactive substance
Real side effects caused by negative expectations
Severe pain triggered by physical nerve damage
The body's natural system for relieving pain
questions.explain: Bài viết định nghĩa nocebo effect là hiện tượng "in which negative expectations produce real side effects", trái ngược với placebo effect mang lại cải thiện tích cực sau khi dùng giả dược.

questions.q: Which factor is said to strengthen the placebo response?
options: A brisk, impersonal clinician
Taking one pill rather than two
Plain, unbranded tablets
A warm, attentive clinician
questions.explain: Bài viết: "patients treated by a warm, attentive clinician frequently report greater improvement" → đáp án đúng: A warm, attentive clinician.

readings.title: Universal Basic Income: Utopia or Necessity?
readings.summaryVi: Thu nhập cơ bản phổ quát hứa hẹn xóa bỏ thủ tục rườm rà và “bẫy phúc lợi”, nhưng chi phí rất lớn; các thí điểm cho kết quả tích cực song chưa đủ để kết luận.
readings.summaryEn: A universal basic income promises to remove complicated paperwork and the "welfare trap", but it is very expensive; pilot schemes have shown positive results that are not yet enough to draw conclusions.
readings.text:
The proposal that every citizen should receive a regular cash payment from the state, regardless of employment or wealth, has a surprisingly long and varied intellectual history. Advocated at different times by radical reformers and free-market economists alike, universal basic income (UBI) has re-emerged in recent years as a response to concerns about automation, insecure work and the complexity of existing welfare systems.

Proponents advance several distinct arguments. First, because the payment is unconditional, it eliminates the bureaucracy involved in assessing eligibility, as well as the stigma that sometimes deters people from claiming support to which they are entitled. Second, it avoids the so-called welfare trap, whereby people who take on paid work lose benefits at such a rate that they gain little or nothing financially. Third, supporters contend that a guaranteed income floor would provide security in a labour market increasingly characterised by short-term contracts and, potentially, by the displacement of jobs through artificial intelligence.

Critics raise equally substantial objections. The most immediate is cost. A payment generous enough to live on, distributed to an entire adult population, would require large increases in taxation or the dismantling of other public services. If, conversely, the payment is set at a modest level, it may be insufficient to replace targeted benefits for people with disabilities or high housing costs, potentially leaving the most vulnerable worse off. Others worry that an unconditional income might weaken the incentive to work, although the strength of this effect is fiercely disputed.

Empirical evidence remains limited, partly because genuinely universal schemes have rarely been tested. Pilot projects in countries including Finland, Kenya and Canada have typically involved selected groups rather than whole populations, and for fixed periods. Their findings have nonetheless been instructive. Recipients have generally reported improved wellbeing and reduced stress, and most studies have found little evidence of a significant decline in employment. Sceptics point out, however, that temporary experiments cannot reveal how behaviour or prices might change if a payment were permanent and nationwide.

Ultimately, the debate about UBI reflects deeper disagreements about the purpose of the welfare state: whether it should primarily provide a safety net for those in need, or guarantee every citizen a baseline of economic independence. Until larger and longer-term trials are conducted, the question is likely to be settled as much by political values as by evidence.

questions.q: Support for UBI has come from people with very different political views.
questions.explain: Bài viết: UBI has been "Advocated at different times by radical reformers and free-market economists alike" → TRUE.

questions.q: Pilot projects have shown a sharp fall in employment among recipients.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "most studies have found little evidence of a significant decline in employment" → FALSE.

questions.q: Finland has decided to introduce UBI for its entire population.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nhắc Phần Lan có dự án thí điểm với nhóm chọn lọc, không nói nước này quyết định áp dụng toàn quốc → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the "welfare trap"?
options: When people who start paid work lose benefits so quickly that they gain little
When people who apply for unemployment relief face excessive official paperwork
When people who lack formal qualifications are unable to secure any employment
When people who live in economically deprived regions must rely on private charity
questions.explain: Theo bài viết, 'welfare trap' là tình trạng người bắt đầu đi làm có lương bị cắt giảm phúc lợi nhanh đến mức hầu như không cải thiện được thu nhập; các đáp án khác chỉ các khó khăn thủ tục hoặc tìm việc làm thông thường.

questions.q: Why do sceptics doubt the results of the pilot projects?
options: The pilots could not be implemented due to insufficient funding at the national level.
The experiments failed to reduce unemployment among participants in the short term.
Temporary experiments cannot show how behaviour or prices would change under a permanent scheme.
The pilots targeted only urban neighborhoods rather than entire regions throughout the country.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "temporary experiments cannot reveal how behaviour or prices might change if a payment were permanent and nationwide" → đáp án đúng: Temporary experiments cannot show how behaviour or prices would change under a permanent scheme..

readings.title: The Slow Pandemic: Antibiotic Resistance
readings.summaryVi: Việc lạm dụng kháng sinh ở người và vật nuôi đẩy nhanh tình trạng vi khuẩn kháng thuốc, trong khi thuốc mới ngày càng ít; cần quản lý kê đơn, chẩn đoán nhanh và mô hình tài trợ mới.
readings.summaryEn: The overuse of antibiotics in people and farm animals speeds up drug resistance in bacteria, while fewer new drugs are being developed; better prescribing, rapid diagnosis and new funding models are needed.
readings.text:
When penicillin entered widespread use in the 1940s, it transformed medicine. Infections that had routinely killed, such as pneumonia, infected wounds and complications of childbirth, suddenly became treatable. Antibiotics also made possible many modern procedures, from major surgery to cancer chemotherapy, which depend on the ability to prevent or control bacterial infection. Yet even Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin, warned that its misuse could render bacteria resistant. That warning has proved remarkably prescient.

Resistance is, at its core, a matter of natural selection. Whenever bacteria are exposed to an antibiotic, the most susceptible are killed, while any that happen to carry a resistance mechanism survive and multiply. Bacteria can also exchange genetic material with one another, allowing resistance to spread between different species. Consequently, every use of an antibiotic, however justified, exerts some selective pressure; unnecessary use simply accelerates the process.

Such unnecessary use is widespread. Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for viral illnesses such as colds and influenza, against which they are entirely ineffective. In some countries they can be purchased without a prescription, and patients who stop a course early or share leftover tablets may contribute further. Agriculture is another major factor: in many parts of the world, large quantities are administered to livestock not to treat disease but to promote growth or to compensate for crowded conditions.

The consequences are already severe. Drug-resistant infections are estimated to be directly responsible for over a million deaths a year, and some strains have emerged that resist almost every available treatment. Compounding the problem, the pipeline of new antibiotics has slowed dramatically. Because new antibiotics would ideally be used sparingly, to preserve their effectiveness, pharmaceutical companies have little prospect of recovering development costs, and many have withdrawn from the field.

Addressing the crisis therefore requires action on several levels. Stewardship programmes in hospitals aim to ensure that antibiotics are prescribed only when necessary and that the right drug is chosen. Rapid diagnostic tests can help clinicians distinguish bacterial from viral infections. Improved sanitation and vaccination reduce the number of infections in the first place. Some governments are experimenting with new funding models, such as paying companies a fixed annual fee for access to a new antibiotic, regardless of how much is sold, thereby separating profit from sales volume.

Because bacteria do not respect borders, no single country can solve the problem alone. Experts describe antimicrobial resistance as a slow-moving pandemic: less visible than a sudden outbreak, but potentially just as dangerous if left unchecked.

questions.q: Alexander Fleming warned that misuse of penicillin could lead to resistance.
questions.explain: Bài viết: Fleming "warned that its misuse could render bacteria resistant" → TRUE.

questions.q: Antibiotics are effective against colds and influenza.
questions.explain: Bài viết: antibiotics are prescribed for colds and influenza, "against which they are entirely ineffective" → FALSE.

questions.q: Most new antibiotics are now developed by universities.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói nhiều công ty dược đã rút khỏi lĩnh vực này, không nhắc đến vai trò của các trường đại học → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why have many pharmaceutical companies withdrawn from developing antibiotics?
options: Clinical trials for infectious illnesses have become strictly forbidden.
Common bacteria rarely cause life-threatening symptoms in patients.
Modern synthesising processes are excessively simple and unpatented.
New antibiotics would be used sparingly, so costs are hard to recover.
questions.explain: Bài đọc nêu rõ vì các loại kháng sinh mới cần được sử dụng hạn chế để tránh kháng thuốc, các hãng dược khó có thể thu hồi chi phí nghiên cứu và phát triển.

questions.q: What is the purpose of paying companies a fixed annual fee?
options: To increase sales of antibiotics
To separate profit from sales volume
To replace vaccination programmes
To promote growth in livestock
questions.explain: Bài viết: the fee is paid "regardless of how much is sold, thereby separating profit from sales volume" → đáp án đúng: To separate profit from sales volume.

readings.title: The Economics of "Free" Shipping
readings.summaryVi: Giao hàng "miễn phí" thực chất có chi phí: được tính vào giá, ngưỡng đơn tối thiểu, gói thành viên; tác động tới hành vi mua sắm, lượng hàng trả lại và môi trường.
readings.summaryEn: "Free" delivery actually has costs: they are built into prices, minimum order thresholds and membership schemes; it affects shopping behaviour, the number of returns and the environment.
readings.text:
Few words are as powerful in online retail as "free shipping". Shoppers are often more willing to pay a slightly higher price for a product with free delivery than a lower price plus a separate shipping fee, even when the total cost is the same. Retailers understand this well, which is why free shipping has become one of the most common features of online shopping.

Of course, delivering a parcel is never actually free. Someone has to pay for warehouses, packaging, fuel and drivers. In practice, retailers recover these costs in several ways. Some build them into the prices of their products. Others set a minimum order value, encouraging customers to add extra items to their basket in order to qualify. Membership programs that offer unlimited free delivery for an annual fee are another strategy; once customers have paid, they tend to shop more often with that retailer to get value from their membership.

Free shipping also changes how people shop. When delivery and returns cost nothing, customers may order several sizes of the same item and send back those that do not fit. Handling returns is expensive for retailers, and many returned products cannot be resold as new.

There are environmental consequences as well. Fast, free delivery encourages frequent small orders, which can mean more half-empty vans on the road and more packaging. In response, some companies now offer customers the option of slower delivery or of grouping orders into a single weekly shipment. Whether shoppers will choose these options when speed is still free remains an open question.

questions.q: Shoppers may prefer a higher price with free delivery to a lower price plus a shipping fee.
questions.explain: Bài viết: người mua thường "more willing to pay a slightly higher price for a product with free delivery than a lower price plus a separate shipping fee" → TRUE.

questions.q: Retailers do not need to pay anything for free deliveries.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "delivering a parcel is never actually free" – phải trả kho, bao bì, nhiên liệu, tài xế → FALSE.

questions.q: Most customers choose slower delivery when it is offered.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói việc khách có chọn giao chậm hay không "remains an open question" – không có thông tin rằng đa số chọn → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: How do minimum order values help retailers?
options: They limit the number of items per purchase.
They require customers to pay a handling fee.
They encourage customers to buy extra items.
They decrease the need for promotional discounts.
questions.explain: Bài viết: ngưỡng đơn tối thiểu khuyến khích khách "add extra items to their basket in order to qualify" → đáp án đúng: They encourage customers to buy extra items..

questions.q: Why are returns a problem for retailers?
options: Customers rarely return items.
Returns increase delivery speed.
Returned items are always damaged.
Returns are expensive and many items cannot be resold as new.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Handling returns is expensive for retailers, and many returned products cannot be resold as new." → đáp án đúng: Returns are expensive and many items cannot be resold as new..

readings.title: Noise: The Invisible Pollutant
readings.summaryVi: Ô nhiễm tiếng ồn ảnh hưởng giấc ngủ, căng thẳng và sức khỏe tim mạch; nguồn chính là giao thông; các giải pháp quy hoạch, vật liệu, quy định và hành vi.
readings.summaryEn: Noise pollution affects sleep, stress levels and heart health; the main source is traffic; solutions include urban planning, materials, regulations and changes in behaviour.
readings.text:
When people think about pollution, they usually imagine dirty air or plastic in the sea. Noise is rarely mentioned, partly because it leaves no visible trace. Yet health authorities, including the World Health Organization, recognize environmental noise as a significant risk to public health, particularly in cities.

The most obvious effect of noise is disturbed sleep. Even when people do not fully wake up, noise from traffic or aircraft at night can interrupt the deeper stages of sleep, leaving them tired the next day. Over time, constant noise is associated with chronic stress, and researchers have linked long-term exposure to higher risks of high blood pressure and heart disease. Children's concentration and learning can also be affected when schools are located near busy roads or airports.

In most cities, the main source of environmental noise is road traffic. This suggests a range of solutions. Lower speed limits reduce tyre and engine noise, and quieter road surfaces can make a noticeable difference. Electric vehicles are much quieter at low speeds, although at higher speeds most of the noise comes from tyres rather than engines. Planners can also place offices or shops, rather than bedrooms, along the busiest streets, and use trees and barriers to absorb sound.

Individual choices matter too, from using headphones on public transport to keeping noisy household tasks to daytime hours. Unlike many environmental problems, noise disappears the moment its source stops – which means that, with the right policies, cities can become quieter remarkably quickly.

questions.q: Noise can disturb sleep even when people do not fully wake up.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Even when people do not fully wake up, noise … can interrupt the deeper stages of sleep" → TRUE.

questions.q: At high speeds, most noise from electric vehicles comes from their engines.
questions.explain: Bài viết: ở tốc độ cao "most of the noise comes from tyres rather than engines" → FALSE.

questions.q: Noise pollution is worse in Europe than in Asia.
questions.explain: Bài viết không so sánh mức ô nhiễm tiếng ồn giữa các châu lục → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the main source of environmental noise in most cities?
options: Aircraft
Construction
Road traffic
Household tasks
questions.explain: Bài viết: "In most cities, the main source of environmental noise is road traffic." → đáp án đúng: Road traffic.

questions.q: Why does the writer say cities can become quieter "remarkably quickly"?
options: Because noise disappears as soon as its source stops
Because noise is louder at night
Because people become accustomed to background sounds
Because planting trees reduces sound instantly
questions.explain: Bài viết: "noise disappears the moment its source stops" nên với chính sách đúng, thành phố có thể yên tĩnh hơn rất nhanh.

readings.title: How the Weekend Was Invented
readings.summaryVi: Cuối tuần hai ngày là phát minh khá mới: từ ngày nghỉ tôn giáo, thói quen "Thứ Hai thánh", phong trào công đoàn đến tuần làm việc 5 ngày ở thế kỷ 20.
readings.summaryEn: The two-day weekend is a fairly recent invention: from religious days of rest and the habit of "Saint Monday" to the trade union movement and the five-day working week of the 20th century.
readings.text:
For most office workers today, the two-day weekend seems like a natural part of life. Historically, however, it is a fairly recent invention. For centuries, many societies observed a single weekly day of rest, usually for religious reasons, while the other six days were working days.

The change began during the Industrial Revolution in Britain. Factory work was long and exhausting, and some workers simply failed to appear on Mondays, a habit that became known jokingly as "Saint Monday". Employers disliked these unpredictable absences, and over time a compromise emerged: workers would come in reliably on Monday in exchange for finishing early on Saturday afternoon. The "half-holiday" on Saturday gradually spread during the nineteenth century, helped by campaigns from trade unions.

In the United States, a major step came in the 1920s, when some large employers introduced a five-day working week for factory workers. The industrialist Henry Ford was among the best known, adopting a five-day, forty-hour week in his factories in 1926. Supporters argued that rested workers were more productive, and that people with free time would also spend more money – including on leisure activities and consumer goods. During the following decades, the two-day weekend became standard across much of the industrialized world.

Today, some companies are experimenting with four-day weeks, and the debate echoes earlier arguments about productivity and well-being. History suggests that the length of the working week is not fixed but reflects the economic and social choices of each era.

questions.q: For centuries, many societies had only one weekly day of rest.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "many societies observed a single weekly day of rest" → TRUE.

questions.q: "Saint Monday" was an official holiday created by employers.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Saint Monday" là cách gọi đùa thói quen công nhân tự nghỉ thứ Hai, và chủ lao động "disliked these unpredictable absences" → không phải ngày nghỉ chính thức → FALSE.
