questions.explain: Bài viết chỉ nói Ford "was among the best known" trong số các chủ lao động áp dụng tuần 5 ngày, không nói ông là người đầu tiên → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What compromise developed between workers and employers in Britain?
options: Workers would work on Sundays for extra pay.
Workers would come on Monday in exchange for finishing early on Saturday.
Employers would close factories on Mondays.
Workers would take a longer lunch break.
questions.explain: Bài viết: công nhân đi làm đều vào thứ Hai "in exchange for finishing early on Saturday afternoon" → đáp án đúng: Workers would come on Monday in exchange for finishing early on Saturday..

questions.q: Which argument did supporters of the five-day week make?
options: Workers would need less training.
Trade unions would become less powerful.
Factories would use less energy.
Rested workers would be more productive and spend more money.
questions.explain: Bài viết: người ủng hộ cho rằng "rested workers were more productive" và người có thời gian rảnh "would also spend more money" → đáp án đúng: Rested workers would be more productive and spend more money..

readings.title: Too Many Choices?
readings.summaryVi: Ý tưởng "mệt mỏi vì quyết định" và "quá nhiều lựa chọn": bằng chứng còn tranh cãi; cách đơn giản hóa lựa chọn hằng ngày một cách thực tế.
readings.summaryEn: The ideas of "decision fatigue" and "too much choice": the evidence is still debated; practical ways to simplify everyday choices.
readings.text:
Modern life involves a remarkable number of decisions, from which of dozens of breakfast cereals to buy to which of hundreds of streaming shows to watch. Some writers argue that this abundance comes at a cost. They point to two popular ideas: that making many decisions gradually wears down our ability to choose well – often called "decision fatigue" – and that having too many options can make people less satisfied, or even unable to choose at all.

Both ideas have intuitive appeal. Most of us have felt exhausted after a long day of choices, or stood in front of a supermarket shelf unsure what to pick. However, the scientific evidence is more mixed than popular articles sometimes suggest. Some well-known experiments have proved difficult to repeat, and reviews of the research suggest that the effect of large choice sets depends heavily on the situation – for example, on whether people already know what they like and how easy the options are to compare.

This does not mean the ideas are useless. Even if the effects are smaller and less universal than once claimed, many people find that reducing unnecessary decisions makes daily life feel calmer. Common strategies include planning meals for the week in advance, keeping a simple routine for mornings, and deciding in advance on a few trusted brands. Businesses, too, have learned that presenting options clearly – with sensible defaults and helpful comparisons – can make customers more comfortable with their choices.

The broader lesson may be that choice itself is neither good nor bad. What matters is whether people have the information and structure they need to choose with confidence.

questions.q: According to the text, the scientific evidence for decision fatigue is completely clear.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the scientific evidence is more mixed than popular articles sometimes suggest" – chưa rõ ràng → FALSE.

questions.q: Some well-known experiments on choice have been difficult to repeat.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Some well-known experiments have proved difficult to repeat" → TRUE.

questions.q: People who plan their meals in advance are healthier.
questions.explain: Bài viết chỉ nói lên kế hoạch bữa ăn giúp cuộc sống "feel calmer", không nói gì về sức khỏe → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to research reviews, what does the effect of large choice sets depend on?
options: The price of the products
The situation, such as whether people know what they like
The time of day
The age of the shoppers
questions.explain: Bài viết: tác động "depends heavily on the situation – for example, on whether people already know what they like and how easy the options are to compare" → đáp án đúng: The situation, such as whether people know what they like.

questions.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: People should avoid making choices.
More choice always makes people happier.
Choice is neither good nor bad; information and structure matter.
Businesses should offer fewer products.
questions.explain: Bài viết kết luận: "choice itself is neither good nor bad. What matters is whether people have the information and structure they need" → đáp án đúng: Choice is neither good nor bad; information and structure matter..

readings.title: The Limits of Falsification
readings.summaryVi: Tiêu chí bác bỏ được của Popper rất thanh nhã nhưng nghiên cứu thực tế hiếm khi tuân theo; vì lý thuyết luôn được kiểm tra cùng các giả định phụ, nó nên là một lý tưởng điều chỉnh hơn là một phép thử máy móc.
readings.summaryEn: Popper's falsifiability criterion is elegant, but real research seldom follows it; because theories are tested with auxiliary assumptions, it works better as a regulative ideal than as a mechanical test.
readings.text:
Few ideas have shaped the popular image of science as profoundly as Karl Popper's claim that a theory is scientific only if it could, in principle, be refuted by observation. The criterion is elegant, and it has the merit of excluding doctrines that accommodate every conceivable outcome. Yet historians of science have long observed that actual research seldom conforms to so austere a model.

Consider what happens when a prediction fails. A theory never confronts the evidence alone; it arrives accompanied by auxiliary assumptions about instruments, background conditions and the behaviour of the materials under study. A discordant result therefore tells us only that something in this whole bundle is mistaken, not which strand should be discarded. In the nineteenth century, irregularities in the orbit of Uranus were met not by abandoning Newtonian mechanics but by postulating an unseen planet, and the gamble paid off with the discovery of Neptune. When an analogous anomaly in Mercury's orbit was blamed on a second hypothetical planet, however, the strategy came to nothing, and the problem was eventually resolved only by a different theory of gravity altogether.

The moral is not that falsifiability is worthless, but that it works better as a regulative ideal than as a mechanical test. Scientists are rational to protect a fruitful theory from a single awkward datum, provided the protective manoeuvres themselves generate new, testable predictions. What distinguishes a healthy research programme from a degenerating one is, on this view, whether its adjustments expand its empirical reach or merely patch over its failures.

questions.q: According to the passage, what does Popper's criterion require of a scientific theory?
options: It must be possible, in principle, to refute it by observation
It must be verified through multiple laboratory tests
It must explain all known phenomena without exception
It must receive unanimous endorsement from the scientific community
questions.explain: Đoạn văn nhấn mạnh tiêu chí falsifiability của Popper là lý thuyết phải có khả năng bị phản bác bằng quan sát, không phải phải đã được lặp lại, dự đoán mọi kết quả, hay được đa số nhà sử học chấp nhận.

questions.q: Why does a failed prediction not simply refute a theory?
options: Researchers often dismiss data that challenge their hypotheses
Measurements are always too imprecise to reveal flaws
Unsuccessful forecasts occur so infrequently they lack significance
The theory is always tested together with auxiliary assumptions
questions.explain: Bài viết: "A theory never confronts the evidence alone" → đáp án đúng: The theory is always tested together with auxiliary assumptions.

questions.q: The search for an unseen planet to explain the orbit of Uranus ultimately succeeded.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the gamble paid off with the discovery of Neptune" → TRUE.

questions.q: The anomaly in the orbit of Mercury was resolved by discovering a second planet.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the problem was eventually resolved only by a different theory of gravity altogether" → FALSE.

questions.q: Popper himself later abandoned the falsifiability criterion.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói về tiêu chí của Popper và những hạn chế của nó, không cho biết chính Popper có từ bỏ tiêu chí này hay không → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: How does the writer suggest falsifiability is best treated?
options: As a regulative ideal rather than a mechanical test
As a mandatory checkpoint that all theories must clear immediately
As a historical notion that no longer influences research
As a principle limited exclusively to astronomical investigations
questions.explain: Bài viết: "it works better as a regulative ideal than as a mechanical test" → đáp án đúng: As a regulative ideal rather than a mechanical test.

questions.q: What distinguishes a healthy research programme from a degenerating one?
options: Whether it avoids making any predictions
Whether it has attracted the largest number of researchers
Whether its adjustments widen its empirical reach rather than merely patch over failures
Whether it keeps its original assumptions unchanged
questions.explain: Bài viết: "whether its adjustments expand its empirical reach or merely patch over its failures" → đáp án đúng: Whether its adjustments widen its empirical reach rather than merely patch over failures.

questions.q: In the first paragraph, "austere" suggests that Popper's model is
options: pleasantly simple and easy to apply
strictly demanding and unadorned
old-fashioned but widely loved
fiercely disputed by scientists
questions.explain: Bài viết: "actual research seldom conforms to so austere a model" → đáp án đúng: strictly demanding and unadorned.

readings.title: Does Language Shape Thought?
readings.summaryVi: Giả thuyết mạnh rằng ngôn ngữ quy định tư duy đã thất bại, còn giả thuyết yếu có bằng chứng nhưng khiêm tốn và còn tranh cãi; ngôn ngữ giống những lối mòn giúp một số hướng nghĩ dễ đi hơn.
readings.summaryEn: The strong claim that language dictates thought has failed, while the weak version has modest but contested evidence; language is better seen as well-worn paths that make some routes of thinking easier.
readings.text:
The proposition that the language we speak shapes the way we think has enjoyed a chequered career. In its strong form, associated with early twentieth-century formulations, it held that speakers of different languages inhabit incommensurable mental worlds, so that certain thoughts are literally unthinkable without the appropriate words. This version has fared poorly. Infants plainly perceive distinctions long before they acquire vocabulary, and translators routinely convey ideas across languages that carve up experience differently.

A weaker thesis has proved far more durable. Experiments suggest that habitual patterns of expression can nudge attention and memory in subtle, measurable ways. Speakers of languages that mark grammatical gender, for instance, sometimes describe the same object with different adjectives depending on whether their language treats it as masculine or feminine. Russian speakers, whose language obliges them to distinguish light from dark blue with separate basic terms, tend to discriminate between those shades marginally faster than English speakers do.

Such effects are real but modest, and their interpretation remains contested. Critics point out that laboratory tasks may themselves invite speakers to consult their linguistic habits, which would exaggerate the influence of language in everyday cognition. Proponents reply that small biases, repeated across countless moments of perception, could accumulate into something more significant. What seems safe to conclude is that language does not imprison thought, yet neither is it a transparent window onto a universal mental reality: it is better understood as a set of well-worn paths that make some routes of thinking easier to follow than others.

questions.q: Why has the strong version of the proposition "fared poorly"?
options: Translators have never managed to convey ideas across languages
No experiment has ever been designed to test it
It was proposed too recently to be assessed
Infants perceive distinctions before they have words for them
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Infants plainly perceive distinctions long before they acquire vocabulary" → đáp án đúng: Infants perceive distinctions before they have words for them.

questions.q: The strong version claims that some thoughts are impossible without the corresponding words.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "certain thoughts are literally unthinkable without the appropriate words" → TRUE.

questions.q: Russian speakers are noticeably slower than English speakers at telling light blue from dark blue.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "tend to discriminate between those shades marginally faster than English speakers do" → FALSE.

questions.q: Bilingual speakers show stronger effects of language on thought than monolingual speakers.
questions.explain: Bài không so sánh người song ngữ với người đơn ngữ → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What does the example of grammatical gender suggest?
options: Habitual grammatical categories may influence which adjectives speakers choose
Masculine objects are always described more positively
Gender is the most important feature of any language
Speakers ignore grammatical gender when they describe objects
questions.explain: Bài viết: "sometimes describe the same object with different adjectives" → đáp án đúng: Habitual grammatical categories may influence which adjectives speakers choose.

questions.q: What is the critics' objection to the experimental evidence?
options: The experiments involved too few languages
The effects were too large to be believable
The participants were all native speakers of English
The tasks may prompt speakers to rely on their language, inflating the effect
questions.explain: Bài viết: "which would exaggerate the influence of language in everyday cognition" → đáp án đúng: The tasks may prompt speakers to rely on their language, inflating the effect.

questions.q: How do proponents answer the critics?
options: Every daily thought operates independently of any linguistic influence
Small biases repeated many times may add up to something significant
Experimental findings consistently mirror everyday actions without deviation
Opponents claim the original studies were never examined thoroughly
questions.explain: Bài viết: "small biases, repeated across countless moments of perception, could accumulate into something more significant" → đáp án đúng: Small biases repeated many times may add up to something significant.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the writer's conclusion?
options: Language has no effect whatsoever on thought
Thought is completely determined by vocabulary
Language neither imprisons thought nor mirrors reality, but eases some paths of thinking
All languages share a single universal way of thinking
questions.explain: Bài viết: "it is better understood as a set of well-worn paths that make some routes of thinking easier to follow than others" → đáp án đúng: Language neither imprisons thought nor mirrors reality, but eases some paths of thinking.

readings.title: When a Measure Becomes a Target
readings.summaryVi: Định luật Goodhart: một chỉ số khi bị biến thành mục tiêu sẽ hết còn đo tốt; bài giải thích cơ chế, ví dụ trong bệnh viện và đại học, và khuyên dùng nhiều chỉ số như gợi ý để tìm hiểu chứ không phải phán quyết.
readings.summaryEn: Goodhart's law: a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure; the article explains the mechanism, with hospital and university examples, and recommends using several indicators as prompts for inquiry.
readings.text:
In 1975 the economist Charles Goodhart observed that any statistical regularity tends to collapse once it is pressed into service for control purposes. The principle, since generalised into the maxim that a measure which becomes a target ceases to be a good measure, explains an astonishing range of institutional pathologies. Hospitals instructed to reduce waiting times have been known to keep patients in ambulances outside the building, where the clock has not yet started. Universities rewarded for publication counts oblige researchers to divide a single study into several slender papers.

The underlying mechanism is not mere cynicism. A metric is a proxy: it stands in for something harder to observe, such as quality of care or depth of scholarship, because the real object resists direct quantification. So long as nobody's livelihood depends on the proxy, it tracks the underlying reality tolerably well. Once rewards and penalties attach to it, however, rational agents redirect their effort toward whatever the indicator captures, and the correlation that made it useful erodes.

None of this implies that organisations should abandon measurement; judgement unaided by evidence has its own, rather well-documented, vices. A more defensible conclusion is that indicators should be plural, difficult to game and treated as prompts for inquiry rather than as verdicts. Managers who ask why a figure has moved, rather than how to move it, preserve the information the number was meant to supply. The temptation to do the opposite is considerable, because a single figure is easy to publish, to compare and to defend, whereas understanding is slow, qualitative and awkward to put on a chart.

questions.q: What did Goodhart observe?
options: A statistical regularity tends to collapse when it is used for control
Governments should avoid gathering statistical data for policy decisions
Economic indicators are frequently misleading when used to predict growth
Hospitals often report waiting times inaccurately to improve public image
questions.explain: Bài viết: "any statistical regularity tends to collapse once it is pressed into service for control purposes" → đáp án đúng: A statistical regularity tends to collapse when it is used for control.

questions.q: Some hospitals have kept patients waiting in ambulances so that waiting-time clocks have not started.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "keep patients in ambulances outside the building" → TRUE.

questions.q: The writer claims that researchers who split studies into several papers are acting out of simple cynicism.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "The underlying mechanism is not mere cynicism" → FALSE.

questions.q: Goodhart spent most of his career working at a central bank.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu Goodhart là nhà kinh tế học và năm 1975 ông đưa ra nhận xét; không nói gì về nơi ông làm việc → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why does the writer describe a metric as a "proxy"?
options: It originates from an external source
It costs less than gathering the actual information
Its application is limited to health and schooling fields
It stands in for something that is hard to measure directly
questions.explain: Bài viết: "because the real object resists direct quantification" → đáp án đúng: It stands in for something that is hard to measure directly.

questions.q: What happens once rewards and penalties are attached to an indicator?
options: People ignore the indicator completely
People redirect effort towards the indicator, weakening its link to reality
The indicator becomes more accurate
Organisations stop collecting data
questions.explain: Bài viết: "rational agents redirect their effort toward whatever the indicator captures" → đáp án đúng: People redirect effort towards the indicator, weakening its link to reality.

questions.q: What does the writer recommend about indicators?
options: Abandon formal metrics in favour of pure qualitative assessment
Select a single straightforward metric to guide organizational policy
Use several that are hard to game and treat them as prompts for inquiry
Tie all financial incentives directly to the most precise indicator
questions.explain: Tác giả khuyên nên dùng nhiều chỉ số khó bị thao túng và xem chúng như gợi ý để tìm hiểu thay vì kết luận (đáp án C). Các phương án A, B, D đi ngược lại lời khuyên duy trì nhiều chỉ số mang tính định hướng này.

questions.q: Why are managers tempted to rely on a single figure?
options: It is easy to publish, compare and defend
It always reflects the truth
Understanding is quick and easy to chart
Regulators forbid the use of other evidence
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a single figure is easy to publish, to compare and to defend" → đáp án đúng: It is easy to publish, compare and defend.

readings.title: The Aura of the Original
readings.summaryVi: Khái niệm "hào quang" của Walter Benjamin nhìn lại sau gần một thế kỷ: bản sao số không xóa hào quang mà còn quảng bá nó, và hào quang có lẽ nằm ở những câu chuyện ta tin hơn là ở vật thể.
readings.summaryEn: Walter Benjamin's "aura" revisited after nearly a century: digital copies have advertised rather than abolished it, and it may reside in the stories we believe rather than in the object.
readings.text:
When Walter Benjamin wrote in the 1930s of the "aura" that withers when a work is mechanically reproduced, he had in mind something more elusive than mere rarity. The aura, as he conceived it, was the unique presence of an object in time and space, its embeddedness in a tradition of ritual and cult that no photograph could transmit. A reproduction, however faithful, could bring a painting to the viewer, but only by detaching it from the place where it had accrued its authority.

Almost a century later the argument looks both prescient and incomplete. The digital image has made masterpieces universally accessible, yet queues outside major museums have lengthened rather than dwindled. Familiarity with a reproduction appears to whet, not satisfy, the desire to stand before the thing itself. One might say that the copy has not abolished the aura so much as advertised it, converting an obscure object into a destination.

It would be unwise, though, to romanticise the original. Much of what visitors prize in a canvas is the knowledge of its provenance, of the hand that made it, and such knowledge is a cultural construction rather than a perceptual fact. Forgers have occasionally deceived experts for years, and the paintings they produced were not seen differently once the deception was exposed; they were merely judged differently. If aura survives, then, it may reside less in the object than in the stories we are prepared to believe about it, and these stories, unlike the pigment, are renewed with every generation of viewers.

questions.q: What did Benjamin mean by the "aura" of a work?
options: The historical significance of the artwork within museums
The intensity of its visual colours and shading
The reputation of the artist who produced the piece
The unique presence of an object in time and space
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the unique presence of an object in time and space" → đáp án đúng: The unique presence of an object in time and space.

questions.q: Why, in Benjamin's view, can a reproduction not carry the aura?
options: It is always of poor technical quality
It detaches the work from the place where it gained its authority
It is seen only by experts
It is too expensive to distribute
questions.explain: Bài viết: "only by detaching it from the place where it had accrued its authority" → đáp án đúng: It detaches the work from the place where it gained its authority.

questions.q: Queues outside major museums have become longer despite the spread of digital images.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "queues outside major museums have lengthened rather than dwindled" → TRUE.

questions.q: Benjamin believed that a good photograph could fully preserve the aura of a painting.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "no photograph could transmit" → FALSE.

questions.q: Benjamin's essay was first published in a German newspaper.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói Benjamin viết vào những năm 1930, không nêu nơi bài được đăng lần đầu → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by saying the copy has "advertised" the aura?
options: Museums have begun funding commercial advertising campaigns
Replicas have taken the place of authentic works in exhibition spaces
Seeing reproductions makes people want to see the original
Authentic pieces have lost their monetary worth over time
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Familiarity with a reproduction appears to whet, not satisfy, the desire to stand before the thing itself" → đáp án đúng: Seeing reproductions makes people want to see the original.

questions.q: What does the example of forgeries show?
options: Experts can always detect a forgery at once
Judgements of a work change with knowledge of its origin, not with what is seen
Forged paintings look worse than originals
Museums should avoid displaying disputed works
questions.explain: Bài viết: "were not seen differently once the deception was exposed; they were merely judged differently" → đáp án đúng: Judgements of a work change with knowledge of its origin, not with what is seen.

questions.q: Where does the writer suggest aura may ultimately reside?
options: In the stories people are willing to believe about the object
In the pigments and canvas that compose the original artwork
In the number of visitors that a museum regularly receives
In the technical quality of the reproduced image or print
questions.explain: Bài viết: "it may reside less in the object than in the stories we are prepared to believe about it" → đáp án đúng: In the stories people are willing to believe about the object.

readings.title: The Dead Hand and the Living Law
readings.summaryVi: Học thuyết án lệ buộc thẩm phán theo các phán quyết cũ nhưng luật vẫn phải thích ứng; kỹ thuật phân biệt vụ việc vừa được ca ngợi vì tính ổn định, vừa bị chỉ trích vì che giấu những lựa chọn giá trị.
readings.summaryEn: The doctrine of precedent binds judges to old decisions while law must adapt; the technique of distinguishing cases is praised for stability and criticised for hiding contested value judgments.
readings.text:
Common-law systems rest upon a principle that can seem faintly paradoxical: judges are bound by decisions made long ago, often in circumstances that no one now living would recognise, and yet the body of law they administer is expected to adapt to a changing society. The doctrine of precedent, known by its Latin tag stare decisis, resolves the tension, if it resolves it at all, through the technique of distinguishing. A court that finds an earlier ruling inconvenient need not overrule it; it may instead identify some material difference of fact that renders the older decision inapplicable.

Defenders of this method praise its restraint. Predictability is itself a form of justice, since citizens arrange their affairs on the assumption that like cases will be treated alike, and a judiciary free to rewrite doctrine at will would resemble a legislature without the discipline of electoral accountability. Gradual adjustment, moreover, allows rules to be tested against concrete disputes rather than imposed in the abstract.

Detractors reply that the pretence of continuity can obscure what is really happening. When a court distinguishes a precedent on grounds so slight that no reasonable observer would find them persuasive, the judgment preserves the form of fidelity while abandoning its substance. The result is a body of case law of bewildering subtlety, accessible only to specialists, and an appearance of inevitability that serves to shield contested value judgments from scrutiny. Whether these costs outweigh the benefits of stability is a question on which jurists continue to disagree, and perhaps ought to.

questions.q: What is the apparent paradox at the heart of common-law systems?
options: Judges may overrule any law they dislike
Courts apply Latin terms that nobody understands
Judges are bound by old decisions, yet the law must adapt to change
Legislatures cannot change decisions made by judges
questions.explain: Bài viết: "judges are bound by decisions made long ago" → đáp án đúng: Judges are bound by old decisions, yet the law must adapt to change.

questions.q: A court can avoid an inconvenient precedent without formally overruling it.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "need not overrule it; it may instead identify some material difference of fact" → TRUE.

questions.q: Defenders claim that judges are answerable to voters in the same way that legislators are.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a legislature without the discipline of electoral accountability" → FALSE.

questions.q: Stare decisis is applied more strictly in the United States than in Britain.
questions.explain: Bài không so sánh mức độ áp dụng nguyên tắc này giữa Mỹ và Anh → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why do defenders regard predictability as "a form of justice"?
options: It suggests lawmakers can abandon the process of drafting statutes
It enables jurists to reach verdicts in a shorter timeframe
It stops attorneys from demanding excessive remuneration
People organise their lives expecting like cases to be treated alike
questions.explain: Bài viết: "citizens arrange their affairs on the assumption that like cases will be treated alike" → đáp án đúng: People organise their lives expecting like cases to be treated alike.

questions.q: What is the detractors' main complaint about distinguishing precedents on slight grounds?
options: It produces legal judgments that are too brief to explain the decision
It keeps the form of fidelity to precedent but not the substance
It compels appellate courts to overrule far too many established cases
It grants legislative bodies excessive oversight over judicial rulings
questions.explain: Những người chỉ trích cho rằng việc phân biệt tiền lệ dựa trên lý do quá nhỏ nhặt sẽ "preserves the form of fidelity while abandoning its substance" (đáp án B). Các đáp án khác đưa ra những lời phàn nàn không được đề cập trong bài.

questions.q: According to the detractors, what does the "appearance of inevitability" achieve?
options: It clarifies the underlying principles of law for laypeople
It restricts judges from revisiting previous decisions
It accelerates judicial proceedings by simplifying case analysis
It protects contested value judgments from close examination
questions.explain: Bài viết: "an appearance of inevitability that serves to shield contested value judgments from scrutiny" → đáp án đúng: It protects contested value judgments from close examination.

questions.q: How does the writer treat the final question about costs and benefits?
options: As settled in favour of stability
As settled in favour of reform
As an open question on which disagreement is appropriate
As too trivial to discuss
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a question on which jurists continue to disagree, and perhaps ought to" → đáp án đúng: As an open question on which disagreement is appropriate.

readings.title: The Invention of Progress
readings.summaryVi: Niềm tin vào tiến bộ không có từ thuở xa xưa mà hình thành ở thế kỷ 17-18; thế kỷ 20 làm nó lung lay, nhưng nó tồn tại vì không phải là một tuyên bố duy nhất.
readings.summaryEn: Belief in progress is not ancient but crystallised in the 17th and 18th centuries; the 20th century shook it, yet it survives because it is not a single claim.
readings.text:
It is tempting to assume that the belief in progress is as old as civilisation, a natural response to the accumulation of tools and knowledge. The historical record suggests otherwise. For most of antiquity, thinkers were more inclined to picture time as cyclical, or as a slow decline from a golden age, than as an ascent. Hesiod lamented the degeneration from gold to iron; Christian theology, for its part, located the decisive event of history in the past and the consummation beyond history altogether.

The conviction that human affairs might improve through collective effort here on earth crystallised only in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and it owed much to the conspicuous success of the new natural philosophy. If Newton could unravel the motions of the heavens, why should the ordering of society resist comparable inquiry? Enlightenment writers such as Condorcet drew the optimistic inference with remarkable confidence, sketching a future of expanding knowledge, diminishing inequality and moral refinement.

The twentieth century dealt this faith heavy blows. Industrialised warfare and genocide made it difficult to sustain the notion that scientific advance and moral advance travel together. Yet the idea has proved resilient, partly because it is not a single claim. One may reasonably maintain that technical capacity grows cumulatively while denying that wisdom does, and much contemporary argument consists of people talking past one another about which sense of progress is at issue. To ask whether history has a direction is thus less a factual question than a request to specify what counts as an improvement, and by whose lights.

questions.q: How did most ancient thinkers picture time, according to the passage?
options: As cyclical or as a decline from a golden age
As a steady ascent towards perfection
As a series of random events
As something controlled by scientific laws
questions.explain: Bài viết: "more inclined to picture time as cyclical, or as a slow decline from a golden age" → đáp án đúng: As cyclical or as a decline from a golden age.

questions.q: The belief that society can improve through human effort took shape in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "crystallised only in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries" → TRUE.

questions.q: Condorcet was pessimistic about the prospects for human society.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "drew the optimistic inference with remarkable confidence" → FALSE.

questions.q: Hesiod's picture of decline was influenced by Persian myths.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói Hesiod than thở về sự suy thoái từ vàng sang sắt, không nhắc đến nguồn ảnh hưởng nào → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why did Newton's success matter for the idea of progress?
options: It implied that scientific breakthroughs could predict political revolutions
It argued that moral doctrines were irrelevant to societal development
It suggested that social order could also be understood through inquiry
It encouraged states to allocate additional resources toward experimental research
questions.explain: Bài viết: "why should the ordering of society resist comparable inquiry" → đáp án đúng: It suggested that social order could also be understood through inquiry.

questions.q: What effect did the twentieth century have on faith in progress?
options: It made it hard to believe that scientific and moral advance go together
It cast doubt on the idea that technical capacity leads to greater wisdom
It led scholars to abandon traditional views of history as a slow decline
It proved conclusively that human affairs improve through collective effort
questions.explain: Bài viết: "industrialised warfare and genocide made it difficult to sustain the notion that scientific advance and moral advance travel together" → đáp án đúng: It made it hard to believe that scientific and moral advance go together.

questions.q: Why, according to the writer, has the idea of progress proved resilient?
options: It has been tested and confirmed by historians
It is protected by religious institutions
It was never seriously criticised
It is not a single claim
questions.explain: Bài viết: "it is not a single claim" → đáp án đúng: It is not a single claim.

questions.q: What is the writer's conclusion about whether history has a direction?
options: It can be settled by collecting more facts
It depends on what we count as an improvement
It is clearly true
It is clearly false
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a request to specify what counts as an improvement, and by whose lights" → đáp án đúng: It depends on what we count as an improvement.

readings.title: Shifting Baselines
readings.summaryVi: Mỗi thế hệ nhà nghiên cứu coi hệ sinh thái mình gặp đầu tiên là bình thường, nên mức chuẩn tụt dần; bài nói về hệ quả cho bảo tồn và vai trò của tư liệu lịch sử.
readings.summaryEn: Each generation of researchers treats the ecosystem it first met as normal, so the baseline sinks; the article covers the consequences for conservation and the role of historical evidence.
readings.text:
In 1995 the fisheries scientist Daniel Pauly described a problem that has since become a touchstone of conservation biology. Each generation of researchers, he noted, takes as its point of reference the state of the ecosystem it first encountered, and therefore regards as normal a condition that its predecessors would have judged grievously depleted. Across several generations, the accepted baseline sinks, and with it the ambition of restoration.

The consequences are easy to illustrate. A diver who first explored a Caribbean reef in the 1980s, after its large predatory fish had already been decimated, sees an abundance of small species and finds nothing amiss. Historical sources, from ships' logs to the records of medieval fishing communities, depict waters teeming with creatures now scarcely seen. Without such evidence, scientists risk setting recovery targets that amount to little more than the preservation of an impoverished present.

The phenomenon is not confined to science. Public expectations shift in the same way, which helps to explain why gradual degradation provokes so little alarm: no single year looks markedly worse than the last, so there is never a moment at which the loss feels urgent. Some ecologists have accordingly turned to archaeology, oral testimony and even old photographs in an effort to reconstruct earlier conditions. Their findings do not dictate what should be restored, since a return to some pristine past is neither feasible nor always desirable, but they at least make it possible to debate the question with open eyes rather than with the amnesia built into individual lifetimes.

questions.q: What problem did Pauly describe?
options: Estimating fish numbers is practically unfeasible
Scientists cannot agree on the important species
Funding for conservation initiatives is insufficient to maintain them
Each generation treats the ecosystem it first saw as the normal state
questions.explain: Bài viết: "takes as its point of reference the state of the ecosystem it first encountered" → đáp án đúng: Each generation treats the ecosystem it first saw as the normal state.

Predatory fish damage coral structures directly in ecosystems

The public typically shows little curiosity about environmental change
No single year looks much worse than the one before
Ecological damage often occurs in remote areas away from humans

Setting recovery targets that merely preserve a depleted present
Focusing exclusively on short-term fluctuation in predatory species
Underestimating the time required for damaged reefs to regenerate

options: Researchers often overlook previous experimental findings
Historical photographs are frequently missing
The public quickly loses recall of past environmental drives
People can only remember what they themselves have experienced
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the amnesia built into individual lifetimes" → đáp án đúng: People can only remember what they themselves have experienced.

readings.title: The Brain as Prediction Machine
readings.summaryVi: Thuyết não là cỗ máy dự đoán đảo ngược mô hình tri giác thụ động: não liên tục đưa ra giả thuyết và chỉ cần báo sai lệch; thuyết hấp dẫn nhưng bị nghi ngờ vì khó bác bỏ.
readings.summaryEn: The brain-as-prediction-machine theory inverts the passive model of perception: the brain generates hypotheses and registers errors; it is attractive but criticised as hard to falsify.
readings.text:
The traditional picture of perception portrays the brain as a passive receiver: light falls on the retina, signals travel inward, and a representation of the world is assembled step by step. A rival account, now ascendant in cognitive neuroscience, inverts the sequence. On this view the brain is fundamentally a prediction engine, continuously generating hypotheses about the causes of its sensory input and using incoming signals chiefly to register where those hypotheses are wrong.

The theory draws support from phenomena that the passive model handles awkwardly. Optical illusions, for example, persist even when we know perfectly well that they are illusions, as though prior expectation were overriding explicit knowledge. A further attraction is efficiency: if only the discrepancy between expectation and reality needs to be transmitted, the volume of information that must travel through the system is greatly reduced. Proponents extend the framework to emotion and even to psychiatric conditions, suggesting that certain disorders reflect predictions that are held too rigidly or too loosely.

Sceptics, however, caution that so capacious a theory risks becoming unfalsifiable. If every observation can be redescribed as the minimisation of prediction error, it is not clear what observation would count against it. The most promising reply is to insist upon precise, mechanistic models whose particular claims about neural circuitry can be tested, and a number of laboratories are now attempting exactly that. Until such work matures, the framework is perhaps best regarded as a fertile organising idea rather than a settled finding.

questions.q: How does the rival account differ from the traditional picture of perception?
options: The brain merely records signals without forming any interpretations
The brain generates hypotheses and uses signals mainly to detect errors
The eyes transmit full pictures straight into long‑term memory
Perception is driven primarily by emotional states, not sensory input
questions.explain: Bài viết: "using incoming signals chiefly to register where those hypotheses are wrong" → đáp án đúng: The brain generates hypotheses and uses signals mainly to detect errors.

questions.q: Optical illusions can persist even when we know that they are illusions.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "persist even when we know perfectly well that they are illusions" → TRUE.

questions.q: On the predictive account, the brain must transmit the full detail of every sensory input.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "only the discrepancy between expectation and reality needs to be transmitted" → FALSE.

questions.q: Most neuroscientists have now abandoned the passive-receiver model.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói cách giải thích mới đang chiếm ưu thế ("ascendant"), không cho biết đa số nhà thần kinh học đã từ bỏ mô hình cũ hay chưa → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What efficiency advantage does the theory offer?
options: Signals propagate more rapidly along neural pathways
The brain uses reduced energy during periods of sleep
Less information needs to travel through the system
Fewer retinal cells are necessary for basic visual perception
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the volume of information that must travel through the system is greatly reduced" → đáp án đúng: Less information needs to travel through the system.

questions.q: How do proponents apply the theory to psychiatric conditions?
options: They suggest some disorders involve predictions held too rigidly or too loosely
They claim that conditions stem from a total failure to register sensory input
They propose that neural circuitry ceases to function during emotional crisis
They argue that mental illnesses are best treated through physical therapy
questions.explain: Bài viết: "suggesting that certain disorders reflect predictions that are held too rigidly or too loosely" → đáp án đúng: They suggest some disorders involve predictions held too rigidly or too loosely.

questions.q: What is the sceptics' main worry?
options: The theory dismisses all previous findings about visual processing in neuroscience
Current experimental methods lack the precision needed to evaluate the theory
It overlooks how emotional states influence perceptual predictions in everyday situations
The theory is so broad that it may be impossible to refute
questions.explain: Bài viết: "risks becoming unfalsifiable" → đáp án đúng: The theory is so broad that it may be impossible to refute.

questions.q: What status does the writer give the framework for now?
options: A universally accepted principle confirmed by numerous experiments
A fertile organising idea rather than a settled finding
A hypothesis that has been disproved by recent studies
A speculative notion limited to philosophical debate
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a fertile organising idea rather than a settled finding" → đáp án đúng: A fertile organising idea rather than a settled finding.

readings.title: Who Answers for the Algorithm?
readings.summaryVi: Khi hệ thống tự động gây hại mà không ai thỏa điều kiện quy trách nhiệm truyền thống, xuất hiện "khoảng trống trách nhiệm"; bài so sánh các quan điểm và cho rằng nghĩa vụ giải trình là điều gần nhất với trách nhiệm có thể đạt được.
readings.summaryEn: When automated systems cause harm and nobody meets the traditional conditions for blame, a "responsibility gap" appears; the article weighs the views and concludes that a duty to give an account is the nearest thing to accountability.
readings.text:
When an automated system denies a mortgage, flags a traveller as a security risk or recommends a prison sentence, the question of who is responsible has no obvious answer. The programmers wrote code they could not fully anticipate in operation; the institution deployed a tool it did not design; the officials who relied on it deferred to an output they were scarcely in a position to challenge. Philosophers have begun to speak of a "responsibility gap", a situation in which harm occurs, yet no individual satisfies the traditional conditions for blame, namely control over the outcome and foreknowledge of it.

Some argue that the gap is illusory, a product of fascination with the technology. We have long attributed responsibility to organisations whose actions cannot be traced to a single agent, and we hold employers liable for the conduct of staff they could not directly supervise. Corporate and institutional liability may therefore suffice, provided regulation insists that those who profit from a system also bear the cost of its errors.

Others consider this too complacent. Where a model learns from data in ways that even its designers cannot interpret, they contend, the notion of foreseeability itself begins to fray, and liability rules built upon it may reward negligence by making ignorance a defence. A growing body of legislation consequently demands documentation, auditing and a right to human review. These measures do not settle the philosophical problem, but they have the practical virtue of ensuring that someone, somewhere, is obliged to give an account, and that obligation may be the nearest thing to accountability that complex systems permit.

questions.q: What is meant by a "responsibility gap"?
options: A time lag exists between system malfunction and its detection
A conflict arises between developers and project overseers
Harm occurs but no one meets the traditional conditions for blame
An absence of specific regulations governing autonomous technologies
questions.explain: Bài viết: "no individual satisfies the traditional conditions for blame" → đáp án đúng: Harm occurs but no one meets the traditional conditions for blame.

questions.q: Traditional blame requires both control over the outcome and foreknowledge of it.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "namely control over the outcome and foreknowledge of it" → TRUE.

questions.q: Those who think the gap is illusory say that organisations can never be held responsible.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "We have long attributed responsibility to organisations" → FALSE.

questions.q: The first law requiring human review of automated decisions was passed in the European Union.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói một loạt luật đang tăng lên đòi hỏi tài liệu, kiểm toán và quyền xem xét của con người, không nêu luật đầu tiên ở đâu → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What conclusion do those who see the gap as illusory reach?
options: Corporate liability may be enough if those who profit bear the cost of errors
Individual programmers must be held accountable for unintended system outputs
Automated decision tools should be entirely removed from high-stakes contexts
Institutional regulations ought to impose strict oversight on software developers
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Corporate and institutional liability may therefore suffice, provided regulation insists that those who profit from a system also bear the cost of its errors" → đáp án đúng: Corporate liability may be enough if those who profit bear the cost of errors.

questions.q: Why do the other critics think liability rules may reward negligence?
options: When designers cannot interpret a model, ignorance can become a defence
Companies deliberately hide how models work
Judges refuse to hear technical evidence
Employers are never liable for staff
questions.explain: Bài viết: "liability rules built upon it may reward negligence by making ignorance a defence" → đáp án đúng: When designers cannot interpret a model, ignorance can become a defence.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, "too complacent" means that the argument is
options: excessively intricate for readers to follow
overly skeptical about technological progress
prematurely introduced without sufficient evaluation
too satisfied that existing arrangements are adequate
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Others consider this too complacent" → đáp án đúng: too satisfied that existing arrangements are adequate.

questions.q: What practical benefit do documentation, auditing and human review bring?
options: They completely eliminate the underlying philosophical dilemma
They guarantee flawless performance of computational models
They ensure that someone is obliged to give an account
They eliminate the necessity for any form of legislative oversight
questions.explain: Bài viết: "ensuring that someone, somewhere, is obliged to give an account" → đáp án đúng: They ensure that someone is obliged to give an account.

readings.title: Eyes on the Street
readings.summaryVi: Jane Jacobs phê phán quy hoạch tách chức năng, cho rằng an toàn đường phố đến từ sự hiện diện thường xuyên của người dân; di sản của bà vừa có ảnh hưởng lớn vừa gây tranh cãi, kể cả hệ quả gentrification.
readings.summaryEn: Jane Jacobs attacked functional zoning, arguing that street safety comes from the constant presence of ordinary people; her legacy is hugely influential yet contested, including gentrification.
readings.text:
Mid-century planning orthodoxy held that cities worked best when their functions were separated: housing here, commerce there, industry elsewhere, all linked by arterial roads and softened by green space. In 1961 Jane Jacobs mounted a celebrated assault on this vision, arguing that it mistook visual order for social health. What makes a street safe, she contended, is not policing or open space but the continuous presence of ordinary people with reasons to be there at different hours: shopkeepers, residents, passers-by. This informal surveillance, which she called "eyes on the street", depends on mixed uses and short blocks that keep pedestrians circulating.

Her influence has been immense, but admirers sometimes overlook the ambiguities of her legacy. The vibrant, fine-grained neighbourhoods she defended proved so attractive that they were colonised by wealthier residents, whose arrival pushed rents beyond the reach of the very communities that had created the vitality. Gentrification is thus, in a sense, the price of her success.

Her method also invites criticism. Jacobs generalised from a handful of districts in a few American cities, and her insistence that planning should emulate the self-organising complexity of living systems rested more on observation and rhetorical force than on systematic evidence. Nevertheless, subsequent research on walkability and mixed-use development has largely vindicated her central intuition. The more difficult lesson, which urban theory is still absorbing, is that the qualities she praised cannot simply be designed into existence; they emerge from patterns of use that planners can encourage but never fully command.

questions.q: What did mid-century planning orthodoxy recommend?
options: Mixing housing, shops and industry on the same streets
Separating the functions of a city into distinct zones
Abolishing roads in city centres
Leaving neighbourhoods to plan themselves
questions.explain: Bài viết: "cities worked best when their functions were separated" → đáp án đúng: Separating the functions of a city into distinct zones.

questions.q: According to Jacobs, what makes a street safe?
options: The frequent presence of law enforcement officers patrolling the neighborhood
The installation of open green spaces to separate residential zones
The construction of wide arterial roads that allow traffic to flow smoothly
The continuous presence of ordinary people with reasons to be there
questions.explain: Bài viết: "What makes a street safe... is not policing or open space but the continuous presence of ordinary people with reasons to be there" → đáp án đúng: The continuous presence of ordinary people with reasons to be there.

questions.q: Jacobs launched her attack on planning orthodoxy in 1961.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "In 1961 Jane Jacobs mounted a celebrated assault on this vision" → TRUE.

questions.q: Jacobs argued that open green space is the main factor in street safety.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "not policing or open space" → FALSE.

questions.q: Jacobs grew up in a fine-grained neighbourhood in New York.
questions.explain: Bài không nói gì về nơi Jacobs lớn lên → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why is gentrification described as "the price of her success"?
options: Her ideas led to the demolition of old districts
The neighbourhoods she praised attracted wealthier residents and rents rose
She profited financially from rising rents
Her critics prevented any development
questions.explain: Bài viết: "pushed rents beyond the reach of the very communities that had created the vitality" → đáp án đúng: The neighbourhoods she praised attracted wealthier residents and rents rose.

questions.q: What criticism is made of her method?
options: She ignored the experience of American cities
She used too many statistics
She generalised from a few districts and relied on observation more than systematic evidence
She never proposed any alternative to zoning
questions.explain: Bài viết: "generalised from a handful of districts in a few American cities" → đáp án đúng: She generalised from a few districts and relied on observation more than systematic evidence.

questions.q: What is described as the "more difficult lesson" for urban theory?
options: Valued urban qualities cannot be designed into existence but emerge from use
Planners must prioritize strict zoning over mixed-use districts in cities
Walkability is irrelevant to economic productivity in urban areas
Mixed-use development should be replaced by single-purpose zones throughout the city
questions.explain: Bài viết: "cannot simply be designed into existence; they emerge from patterns of use" → đáp án đúng: Valued urban qualities cannot be designed into existence but emerge from use.

readings.title: Does Language Shape Thought?
readings.summaryVi: Giả thuyết cho rằng ngôn ngữ định hình tư duy từng bị bác bỏ rồi được xem xét lại dưới dạng nhẹ hơn: ngôn ngữ ảnh hưởng đến chú ý và trí nhớ chứ không giam hãm nhận thức.
readings.summaryEn: The claim that language shapes thought was once dismissed and later revived in a weaker form: language nudges attention and memory rather than imprisoning cognition.
readings.text:
Few ideas in the human sciences have had such a turbulent career as linguistic relativity, the proposition that the language one speaks influences how one thinks. In its strongest formulation, popularly associated with Benjamin Lee Whorf, it held that speakers of different languages inhabit incommensurable mental worlds. This deterministic version collapsed under scrutiny: infants plainly reason before they speak, and translators routinely convey ideas across linguistic boundaries, which would be impossible if thought were wholly captive to grammar.

Yet the idea was never entirely interred. In recent decades, experimentalists have resurrected it in a chastened form. Languages that describe space in absolute terms, such as north and south, rather than relative terms such as left and right, appear to produce speakers who keep an unusually precise sense of direction even indoors. Languages that mark obligatory distinctions between, say, light and dark blue seem to sharpen speakers' ability to discriminate those shades fractionally faster.

The crucial qualification is that these effects are modest, context-dependent and, above all, reversible. Bilinguals shift their performance according to the language in which a task is administered, which suggests that language operates less as a cage than as a habit of attention, a groove along which thought tends to run when no other consideration intervenes. The relevant question, then, is no longer whether language constrains what can be thought, but which aspects of experience it makes habitually salient, and at what cost to others.

questions.q: The strongest version of linguistic relativity is still accepted by most researchers today.
questions.explain: Bài viết: phiên bản mạnh "collapsed under scrutiny" (sụp đổ khi bị xem xét kỹ) → FALSE.

questions.q: Speakers of languages that use compass directions may keep a precise sense of direction indoors.
questions.explain: Bài viết: những ngôn ngữ dùng north/south "appear to produce speakers who keep an unusually precise sense of direction even indoors" → TRUE.

questions.q: Whorf conducted experiments with bilingual speakers in several countries.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nhắc Whorf gắn với phiên bản mạnh của giả thuyết, không nói ông thí nghiệm với người song ngữ → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention translators?
options: To illustrate the challenges of preserving cultural nuance
To argue against a deterministic view of language and thought
To highlight errors in literal translation of Whorf
To examine how translation influences language acquisition
questions.explain: Dịch giả truyền đạt ý tưởng qua ranh giới ngôn ngữ, điều không thể xảy ra nếu tư duy hoàn toàn bị ngữ pháp giam giữ → đáp án đúng: To argue against a deterministic view of language and thought.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about the effects of language on thought?
options: They are permanent and unavoidable.
They have never been demonstrated.
They are limited and can change with the language used.
They only affect children.
questions.explain: Bài viết: các hiệu ứng "modest, context-dependent and, above all, reversible", và người song ngữ đổi kết quả theo ngôn ngữ làm bài → đáp án đúng: They are limited and can change with the language used.

readings.title: The Commons Revisited
readings.summaryVi: Mô hình "bi kịch của tài sản chung" tưởng như không thể tránh khỏi, nhưng nghiên cứu thực địa cho thấy nhiều cộng đồng tự xây dựng quy tắc để quản lý tài nguyên bền vững.
readings.summaryEn: The "tragedy of the commons" seemed inevitable, but field research shows that many communities devise their own rules to manage shared resources sustainably.
readings.text:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised a parable that has haunted environmental policy ever since. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each, reasoning rationally, adds one more animal, since the benefit accrues entirely to him while the cost of overgrazing is spread among everyone. The inevitable outcome is ruin. For decades this logic served as a justification for two remedies: either privatise the resource or place it under centralised state control.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom made her reputation by asking an inconvenient question: if the tragedy is inescapable, why do so many commons survive? Studying Alpine meadows, Japanese forests and irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, she documented communities that had husbanded shared resources for centuries without either a landlord or a distant bureaucracy. What distinguished them was not altruism but institutional design: clearly defined boundaries, rules adapted to local conditions, inexpensive means of resolving disputes, graduated penalties for those who cheat, and, crucially, a say for the people affected in the making of the rules.

Her work did not refute Hardin so much as expose the hidden assumption in his parable, namely that the herders cannot communicate. Where they can talk, monitor one another and sanction defectors, cooperation is not a miracle but a predictable equilibrium. This is not to say that every commons can be saved; large, anonymous and fast-changing systems, such as the atmosphere, lack precisely the features that sustain local arrangements. Ostrom's legacy is therefore a more demanding kind of realism, one that treats governance as something to be designed rather than something to be either assumed or abandoned.

questions.q: In Hardin's parable, each herder gains the full benefit of an extra animal but shares the cost of overgrazing.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the benefit accrues entirely to him while the cost of overgrazing is spread among everyone" → TRUE.

questions.q: Ostrom found that successful commons depended mainly on the generosity of individual members.
questions.explain: Bài viết: điều phân biệt các cộng đồng này "was not altruism but institutional design" → FALSE.

questions.q: Ostrom received an international prize for her research on irrigation systems.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói bà nghiên cứu hệ thống tưới tiêu, không nhắc đến giải thưởng nào → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What does the writer identify as the hidden assumption in Hardin's parable?
options: That the herders cannot communicate
That herders are irrational
That the pasture is too small
That the state is unwilling to intervene
questions.explain: Bài viết: giả định ẩn là "the herders cannot communicate" → đáp án đúng: That the herders cannot communicate.

questions.q: According to the passage, why might the atmosphere be difficult to manage as a commons?
options: Scientists disagree about its condition.
It belongs to no country.
It cannot be measured.
It lacks the features that make local arrangements work.
questions.explain: Bài viết: hệ thống lớn, vô danh, thay đổi nhanh như khí quyển "lack precisely the features that sustain local arrangements" → đáp án đúng: It lacks the features that make local arrangements work.

readings.title: The Brain That Rewires Itself
readings.summaryVi: Khả năng tự điều chỉnh của não, từ tái tổ chức vùng vỏ não sau tổn thương đến lập trình lại khi học kỹ năng mới, nhưng cũng bị thổi phồng bởi các sản phẩm "rèn luyện trí não".
readings.summaryEn: The brain's capacity to reorganise itself, from cortical remapping after injury to learning new skills, is real, but it is also exaggerated by commercial "brain-training" products.
readings.text:
For much of the twentieth century, neuroscience held that the adult brain was essentially fixed: neurons, once lost, were irreplaceable, and the circuitry laid down in childhood was immutable. The accumulated evidence of the past thirty years has dismantled that orthodoxy. Following a stroke, undamaged regions can assume functions previously handled by injured tissue. In people who lose their sight, areas normally devoted to vision are recruited for touch and hearing. London taxi drivers, who must memorise a labyrinth of streets, develop a measurably enlarged hippocampus, a region implicated in spatial memory.

Such findings gave rise to the term neuroplasticity, and with it a cottage industry. Companies now promise that a few minutes of daily puzzles will sharpen memory, stave off dementia and raise intelligence. The evidence for such claims is, to put it charitably, thin. People certainly improve at the games they practise, but the gains tend to be narrow and rarely transfer to unrelated abilities, a point confirmed by several large reviews.

The sober reading is that plasticity is a general property of the nervous system, not a lever that can be pulled at will. It is greatest in early life, diminishes with age and responds most reliably to sustained, effortful engagement with demanding and varied tasks, such as learning a language or a musical instrument, rather than to brief, repetitive exercises. The brain adapts to what it is asked to do; the difficulty lies in persuading it to adapt in ways that matter.

questions.q: Until recently, scientists generally believed that the adult brain could not change.
questions.explain: Bài viết: nhiều thập kỷ thế kỷ XX, ngành thần kinh học cho rằng não người lớn "essentially fixed" → TRUE.

questions.q: Brain-training games reliably improve people's performance on unrelated mental tasks.
questions.explain: Bài viết: lợi ích thường hẹp và "rarely transfer to unrelated abilities" → FALSE.

questions.q: Learning a musical instrument can reverse the symptoms of dementia.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu học nhạc cụ là hoạt động đòi hỏi nỗ lực, không nói gì về đảo ngược chứng mất trí → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the example of London taxi drivers?
options: To show that memory declines with age
To illustrate that the brain can change through experience
To criticise the cost of training
To prove that stroke recovery is fast
questions.explain: Tài xế taxi học thuộc mê cung đường phố và hippocampus lớn hơn đo được, minh họa não thay đổi theo trải nghiệm → đáp án đúng: To illustrate that the brain can change through experience.

questions.q: According to the writer, what kind of activity produces the most reliable plasticity?
options: Short, repeated exercises
Passive listening
Sustained and demanding activity
Competitive games
questions.explain: Bài viết: phản ứng đáng tin nhất với "sustained, effortful engagement with demanding and varied tasks" → đáp án đúng: Sustained and demanding activity.

readings.title: The Myth of the Untranslatable Word
readings.summaryVi: Những danh sách "từ không thể dịch" rất hấp dẫn nhưng gây hiểu lầm: mọi khái niệm đều có thể diễn đạt, chỉ là mất nhiều từ hơn và mất sắc thái.
readings.summaryEn: Lists of "untranslatable words" are charming but misleading: any concept can be expressed, though it may take more words and lose some nuance.
readings.text:
Every few months, a list of "untranslatable" words goes viral: the Portuguese saudade, the Japanese komorebi, the German Schadenfreude. Each is presented as proof that some peoples feel what others cannot even name. The charm of such lists is undeniable; their implications are largely spurious.

To begin with, nobody has ever suggested that English speakers are incapable of feeling pleasure at another's misfortune; we have simply borrowed the German word for it, as we have borrowed many others. What differs between languages is not the repertoire of human experience but the packaging, that is, which experiences are bundled into a single word and which require a phrase. The Japanese komorebi, sunlight filtering through leaves, loses nothing conceptually when rendered in English, only brevity.

Translators know that genuine difficulty lies elsewhere. A pun, a rhyme, a register of formality or the cultural associations of a dish cannot be carried across by dictionary equivalence, and the translator must choose what to sacrifice. Paradoxically, the very word "untranslatable" is a poor description of this predicament, since the same texts are translated every day, albeit imperfectly. Perhaps it would be more accurate, and certainly more modest, to say that translation is never lossless but rarely impossible, and that the most interesting words are not those with no equivalent, but those whose equivalents leave something unsaid.

readings.title: After the Black Death
readings.summaryVi: Đại dịch hạch thế kỷ XIV giết hàng chục triệu người nhưng cũng làm thay đổi cán cân quyền lực: lao động khan hiếm, tiền công tăng, chế độ nông nô suy yếu.
readings.summaryEn: The fourteenth-century plague killed tens of millions yet shifted the balance of power: labour became scarce, wages rose and serfdom weakened.
readings.text:
Between 1347 and 1351, the plague swept across Europe with a ferocity that defies easy comprehension; contemporary estimates suggest that between a third and a half of the population perished. It would be perverse to describe such a catastrophe as beneficial, and historians are wary of the temptation to find silver linings in mass death. Yet the demographic collapse indisputably altered the economic order.

Before the epidemic, land was scarce and labour abundant, a condition that favoured landowners, who could extract rents and services from peasants with few alternatives. Afterwards, the ratio was inverted. Fields lay untended, and surviving workers discovered that their labour commanded a premium. In England, the authorities responded with the Ordinance of Labourers in 1349, which attempted to freeze wages at pre-plague levels. The legislation was widely evaded; employers desperate for hands paid more regardless, and the statute became an object of resentment that contributed to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

The long-term consequences varied by region. In western Europe, serfdom, already eroding, declined sharply as tenants bargained for money rents in place of obligatory labour. In parts of eastern Europe, by contrast, landlords responded to scarcity by tightening their control, and serfdom intensified for several centuries. The same shock, in other words, produced opposite outcomes depending on the relative strength of those who owned the land and those who worked it, a reminder that demography shapes history only through the institutions that mediate it.

questions.q: Historians are generally cautious about describing the Black Death as having positive effects.
questions.explain: Bài viết: các sử gia "are wary of the temptation to find silver linings in mass death" → TRUE.

questions.q: The Ordinance of Labourers succeeded in keeping wages at their pre-plague level.
questions.explain: Bài viết: đạo luật "was widely evaded; employers ... paid more regardless" → FALSE.

questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói đạo luật góp phần gây ra cuộc nổi dậy, không nêu ai lãnh đạo → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What happened to the balance between land and labour after the plague?
options: Labour became scarce relative to land.
Land became scarce relative to labour.
Both became equally abundant.
It stayed the same.
questions.explain: Bài viết: trước dịch đất khan hiếm, lao động dồi dào; sau đó "the ratio was inverted" → đáp án đúng: Labour became scarce relative to land.

questions.q: What point does the final paragraph make about serfdom?
options: Serfdom vanished uniformly across all regions within a few decades.
The pandemic had no influence on the status of serf labor.
The effect of the plague depended on local institutions and power.
It was formally ended by the 1350 Statute of Manorial Duties.
questions.explain: Bài viết: cùng một cú sốc cho ra kết quả trái ngược tùy sức mạnh tương đối của địa chủ và người lao động → đáp án đúng: The effect of the plague depended on local institutions and power.

readings.title: Form, Function and the Fate of Concrete
readings.summaryVi: Kiến trúc Brutalist từng được ca ngợi vì sự trung thực của vật liệu, sau đó bị ghét bỏ, rồi nay được bảo tồn trở lại; cuộc tranh luận phản ánh câu hỏi ai quyết định điều gì là đẹp.
readings.summaryEn: Brutalist architecture was praised for honesty of materials, then reviled, and is now being preserved again; the debate reflects the question of who decides what is beautiful.
readings.text:
Few architectural styles have inspired such polarised affections as Brutalism. The name derives from the French béton brut, raw concrete, and its practitioners in the postwar decades regarded the unconcealed material as a moral stance: buildings, they argued, should declare how they are made rather than cloak themselves in decorative veneer. Housing estates, libraries and universities rose in sculptural masses of poured concrete, expressing a confident faith in public institutions.

That faith proved difficult to sustain. Concrete weathers unevenly, streaked by rain and stained by pollution, and many of the buildings were poorly maintained once the optimism that produced them had evaporated. By the 1980s, they were widely denounced as cold and oppressive, and demolition was the preferred fate of many, sometimes to the relief of the residents and sometimes to their dismay.

The pendulum has since swung. A younger generation, unburdened by the original associations, finds in these structures a bold integrity, and campaigns to list threatened buildings have gained momentum. Preservationists confront genuine dilemmas, however. Concrete is notoriously difficult to repair without altering its appearance, and its production generates considerable carbon emissions, so adapting a building may be more sustainable than replacing it, while demolishing it forfeits the energy already invested.

What the controversy reveals is how contingent aesthetic judgement is. A building does not change, yet the verdict on it can reverse within a generation, which should counsel humility to anyone confident that taste is settled.

questions.q: The name Brutalism comes from a French phrase meaning raw concrete.
questions.explain: Bài viết: tên gọi bắt nguồn từ "béton brut, raw concrete" → TRUE.

questions.q: All residents were pleased when Brutalist buildings were demolished.
questions.explain: Bài viết: việc phá dỡ đôi khi khiến cư dân nhẹ nhõm "and sometimes to their dismay" (có lúc họ thất vọng) → FALSE.
